acts|23|34.text: 23:34 asked of what province he was—the letter describing him as a Roman citizen.

esther|4|15.text: 4:15 This pressing monition produced its result. Esther returned answer to Mordochai: "Go, gather together all the Jews that are found in Susa, and fast ye for me: I also and my maidens will fast; and so will I go to the king against the law; and if I perish, I perish." Esther resolves to go to the king unsummoned, but begs Mordochai and all the Jews to unite in a three days' fast, during which she and her maidens will also fast, to seek by earnest humiliation God's gracious assistance in the step she proposes to take, for the purpose of averting the threatened destruction of her people.

esther|4|17.text: 4:17 And Mordochai went his way, i.e., from the place before the court of the king, to do what the queen had commanded him to do.

exodus|12|50.text: 12:50 Exo 12:50 closes the instructions concerning the Passover with the statement that the Israelites carried them out, viz., in after times (e.g., Num 9:5); and in Exo 12:51 the account of the exodus from Egypt is also brought to a close. All that Jehovah promised to Moses in Exo 6:6 and Exo 6:26 had now been fulfilled. But although v. 51 is a concluding formula, and so belongs to the account just closed, Abenezra was so far right in wishing to connect this verse with the commencement of the following chapter, that such concluding formulae generally serve to link together the different incidents, and therefore not only wind up what goes before, but introduce what has yet to come.

exodus|16|11.text: 16:11 And the Lord spake unto Moses,.... Out of the bright and glorious cloud: saying; as follows:

exodus|26|35.text: 26:35 The two other things (already described) were to be placed outside the curtain, viz., in the holy place; the candlestick opposite to the table, the former on the south side of the dwelling, the latter towards the north.

exodus|38|11.text: 38:11 sockets—mortices or holes in which the end of the pillars stood.

exodus|38|17.text: 38:17 The hooks - and their fillets - The capitals, and the silver bands that went round them; see Clarke's note on Exo 26:32.

ezra|2|70.text: 2:70 Dwelt in their cities - They all went to those cities which belonged originally to their respective families.

ezra|10|23.text: 10:23 Of Levites, only six names are given, and that without stated the houses to which they belonged. From Ezr 2:40, however, it appears that they were of the sons of Jeshua and Kadmiel there mentioned. "Kelaiah, the same is Kelita;" the latter is the usual name of the person in question, and that which he bears in Neh 8:7 and Neh 10:11. Jozabad also reappears in Neh 8:7.

ezra|10|24.text: 10:24 Of singers one, and of porters three names are given; comp. Ezr 2:41-42. In all, ten Levites.

genesis|6|21.text: 6:21 Of all food that is eaten - That is, of the food proper for every species of animals.

i-chronicles|1|17.text: 1:17 Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Meshech—or, "Mash"; these were the children of Aram, and grandsons of Shem (Gen 10:23).

i-chronicles|1|18.text: 1:18 Arphaxad begat Shelah—Cainan, the father's name, is omitted here. (See Luke 3:36).

i-chronicles|1|22.text: 1:22 Ebal, and Abimael, and Sheba: Three more of Joktan's thirteen sons (cp. Gen 10:28). The name Ebal is given here as a variant of Obal in Genesis — minor textual variation common in ancient name-lists. Sheba founded a southern Arabian people later famed for its queen who visited Solomon (1 Kgs 10:1) and its merchants (Ezek 27:22).

i-chronicles|1|23.text: 1:23 And Ophir - "Whence gold is brought." And Havilah; "whence pearls are brought." - T.

i-chronicles|2|52.text: 2:52 Shobal - had sons - "Disciples and priests, to whom belonged the half of the oblations." - T.

i-chronicles|6|42.text: 6:42 The son of Ethan, the son of Zimmah, the son of Shimei: A link in the Gershonite Levitical line ascending toward Asaph (6:39-43). The Ethan here is distinct from the Merarite Ethan of 6:44, though the name is shared. Tribal genealogies preserved overlapping names without confusion within their communities.

i-chronicles|14|17.text: 14:17 Into all lands - That is, all the surrounding or neighboring lands and nations, for no others can possibly be intended.

i-chronicles|17|15.text: 17:15 According to all . . . this vision—The revelation of the divine will was made to the prophet in a dream.

i-chronicles|20|6.text: 20:6 Fingers and toes were four and twenty - See the note on 2 Sam 21:20.

i-chronicles|21|11.text: 21:11 Choose thee, &c.—To the three evils these correspond in beautiful agreement: three years, three months, three days [BERTHEAU]. (See on 2 Sam 24:13).

i-chronicles|21|12.text: 21:12 Three days - the pestilence in the land - In 2 Sam 24:13 (note), seven years of famine are mentioned.

i-chronicles|21|24.text: 21:24 For the full price - That is, six hundred shekels full weight of pure gold.

i-chronicles|25|10.text: 25:10 The third to Zaccur, he, his sons, and his brethren, were twelve: The lot-cast assignment for the third musical course goes to Zaccur, Asaph's firstborn (cp. 25:2). Each course consisted of twelve men — the family head plus his sons and brothers — matching the twelve-tribe symmetry that pervades temple administration (cp. 1 Kgs 18:31).

i-chronicles|25|11.text: 25:11 The fourth to Izri, he, his sons, and his brethren, were twelve: The fourth course belonged to Izri (also spelled Zeri in 25:3), one of Jeduthun's six sons. The careful enumeration honored each family equally — no son of Heman, Asaph, or Jeduthun took precedence by birth order; lot-casting placed them as the Lord chose (cp. Prov 16:33).

i-chronicles|25|14.text: 25:14 Jesharelah - Supposed to be the same with Uzziel, son of Heman.

i-kings|16|30.text: 16:30 Whereas the former kings of Israel had only perpetuated the sin of Jeroboam, i.e., the calf-worship. or worship of Jehovah under the image of an ox, which he had introduced, Ahab was not satisfied with this. לכתּו הנקל ויהי, "it came to pass, was it too little?" i.e., because it was too little (cf. Ewald, 362, a.) to walk in the sins of Jeroboam, that he took as his wife Jezebel, the daughter of Ethbaal the king of the Sidonians, and served Baal, and worshipped him.

ii-chronicles|1|5.text: 1:5 The brasen altar that Bezaleel the son of Uri had made, he put before the tabernacle: Solomon's worship at Gibeon used the original wilderness altar (cp. Exod 38:1-2), preserved across centuries. The detail emphasizes continuity — Solomon offered on the same altar Bezalel fashioned at Sinai, anchoring the new monarchy's piety in Mosaic order (cp. 1 Kgs 3:4).

ii-chronicles|1|13.text: 1:13 Here is, 1. Solomon's entrance upon the government (2 Chr 1:13): He came from before the tabernacle, and reigned over Israel. He would not do any acts of government till he had done his acts of devotion, would not take honour to himself till he had given honour to God - first the tabernacle, and then the throne. But, when he had obtained wisdom from God, he did not bury his talent, but as he received the gift ministered the same, did not give up himself to ease and pleasure, but minded business: he reigned over Israel.

ii-chronicles|3|14.text: 3:14 The veil between the holy place and the most holy, not mentioned in Kg1 6:21, was made of the same materials and colours as the veil on the tabernacle, and was inwoven with similar cherub figures; cf. Exo 26:31. וּבוּץ כּרמיל as in 2 Chr 2:13. עלה על, to bring upon; an indefinite expression for: to weave into the material.

ii-chronicles|4|8.text: 4:8 A hundred basons of gold - These were doubtless a sort of paterae or sacrificial spoons, with which they made libations.

ii-chronicles|5|4.text: 5:4 Instead of הלויּם, we have in 2 Kings הכּהנים, the priests bare the ark; and since even according to the Chronicle (2 Chr 5:7) the priests bare the ark into the holy place, we must understand by הלויּם such Levites were also priests. - In 2 Chr 5:5, too the words הלויּם הכּהנים are inexact, and are to be corrected by Kg1 8:4, והלויּם הכּהנים. For even if the Levitic priests bare the ark and the sacred utensils of the tabernacle into the temple, yet the tabernacle itself (the planks, hangings, and coverings of it) was borne into the temple, to be preserved as a holy relic, not by priests, but only by Levites.

ii-chronicles|6|12.text: 6:12 Solomon had, in the foregoing verses, signed and sealed, as it were, the deed of dedication, by which the temple was appropriated to the honour and service of God. Now here he prays the consecration-prayer, by which it was made a figure of Christ, the great Mediator, through whom we are to offer all our prayers, and to expect all God's favours, and to whom we are to have an eye in every thing where we have to do with God.

ii-chronicles|8|9.text: 8:9 שׁלישׁיו ושׁרי should be altered into ושׁלישׁיו שׂריו as in Kg1 9:22, for שׁלישׁים are not chariot combatants, but royal adjutants; see on Exo 14:7 and 2 Sam 23:8. Over the statute labourers 250 upper overseers were placed. נציבים שׂרי, chief of the superiors, i.e., chief overseer. The Keth. נציבים, praefecti, is the true reading; cf. 1 Chr 18:13; 2 Chr 17:2. The Keri has arisen out of Kg1 9:23. These overseers were Israelites, while in the number 550 (Kg1 9:23) the Israelite and Canaanite upper overseers are both included;

ii-chronicles|8|10.text: 8:10 two hundred and fifty that bare rule—(Compare Kg1 9:23). It is generally agreed that the text of one of these passages is corrupt.

ii-chronicles|9|22.text: 9:22 In 2 Chr 9:22-28, all that remained to be said of Solomon's royal glory, his riches, his wisdom, and his revenues, is in conclusion briefly summed up, as in Kg1 10:23-29. From 2 Chr 9:25 onwards, the account given in the Chronicle diverges from that in Kg1 10:26., in so far that what is narrated in Kg1 10:26-28 concerning Solomon's chariots and horses, and his trade with Egypt in horses, is here partly replaced by statements similar in import to those in 1 Kings 5, because the former matters had been already treated of in Chr.

ii-chronicles|10|3.text: 10:3 And they sent—rather, "for they had sent," &c. This is stated as the reason of Jeroboam's return from Egypt.

ii-chronicles|10|12.text: 10:12 We may learn here, 1. That when public affairs are in a ferment violent proceedings do but make bad worse. Rough answers (such as Rehoboam here gave) do but stir up anger and bring oil to the flames. The pilot has need to steer steadily in a storm. Many have been driven to the mischief they did not intend by being too severely dealt with for what they did intend. 2. That, whatever the devices and designs of men are, God is, by all, doing his own work, and fulfilling the word which he has spoken, no iota or tittle of which shall fall to the ground.

ii-chronicles|12|14.text: 12:14 Now the acts of Rehoboam,.... Of these two verses; see Gill on Kg1 14:29. Kg1 14:30. Kg1 14:31. Next: 2 Chronicles Chapter 13

ii-chronicles|12|15.text: 12:15 Close of his reign. On the authorities, see the Introduction, and in reference to the other statements, the commentary on Kg1 14:29-31. מלחמות, wars, i.e., a state of hostility, was between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all days, can only be understood of the hostile attitude of the two rulers to each other, like מלחמה in Kings; for we have no narrative of wars between them after Rehoboam had abandoned, at the instance of the prophet, his proposed war with the Israelites at the commencement of his reign.

ii-chronicles|12|16.text: 12:16 Abijah his son - Concerning the many varieties in this king's name, see the note on Kg1 14:31.

ii-chronicles|16|3.text: 16:3 There is a league - Let there be a treaty, offensive and defensive, between me and thee: see on Kg1 15:22 (note).

ii-chronicles|16|11.text: 16:11 The end of Asa's reign; cf. Kg1 15:23-24. - On 2 Chr 16:11, cf. the Introduction. 2 Chr 16:12-13 In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa became diseased in his feet, and that in a high degree. The words חיו עד־למעלה are a circumstantial clause: to a high degree was his sickness. "And also in his sickness (as in the war against Baasha) he sought not Jahve, but turned to the physicians." דּרשׁ is primarily construed with the accus., as usually in connection with יהוה or אלהים, to seek God, to come before Him with prayer and supplication;

ii-chronicles|18|4.text: 18:4 This is almost word for word the same with what we had, 1 Kings 22. We will not repeat what was there said, nor have we much to add, but may take occasion to think, 1. Of the great duty of acknowledging God in all our ways and enquiring at his word, whatever we undertake. Jehoshaphat was not willing to proceed till he had done this, 2 Chr 18:4. By particular believing prayer, by an unbiased consultation of the scripture and our own consciences, and by an observant regard to the hints of providence, we may make such enquiries and very much to our satisfaction.

ii-chronicles|21|7.text: 21:7 To give a light to him - To give him a descendant.

ii-chronicles|23|9.text: 23:9 Jehoiada the priest delivered to the captains of hundreds spears, and bucklers: The priestly armory included weapons of David (cp. 2 Sam 8:7-12), preserved in the temple as votive offerings. Jehoiada distributes them for the coup that crowns the boy Joash — a moment when sacred space yielded its dedicated arms to protect the rightful Davidic heir.

ii-chronicles|23|15.text: 23:15 They laid hands on her, and when she was come to the entering of the horse gate: Athaliah's execution is removed from the temple precincts to honor the holiness of the house (cp. 23:14). *Sha'ar hassusim* — the horse gate — opened onto the royal stables east of the temple, an appropriate civil location for the queen-usurper's death.

ii-chronicles|29|2.text: 29:2 He did that which was right - See the note on Kg2 18:3.

ii-chronicles|32|32.text: 32:32 The vision of Isaiah - See this prophet, 2 Chronicles 36-39.

ii-chronicles|33|23.text: 33:23 Trespassed more and more - He appears to have exceeded his father, and would take no warning.

ii-chronicles|34|22.text: 34:22 Hilkiah, and they that the king had appointed, went to Huldah the prophetess: The royal embassy bypasses Jeremiah (already prophesying at this time; cp. Jer 1:2) and consults Huldah. Her standing as *nevi'ah* (prophetess) gave her authority to interpret the rediscovered law — placing a woman in the chain of prophetic transmission at one of the kingdom's pivotal moments (cp. Judg 4:4).

ii-chronicles|34|33.text: 34:33 But not only his own subjects did Josiah induce to act towards God in accordance with the covenant; in all the districts of the sons of Israel he removed the idolatrous abominations, and compelled every one in Israel to serve Jahve. The "sons of Israel," as distinguished from the inhabitants of Jerusalem and Benjamin (2 Chr 34:32), are the remnant of the ten tribes in their land, where Josiah, according to 2 Chr 34:6., had also destroyed the idolatrous places of worship and the images.

ii-chronicles|36|4.text: 36:4 The king of Egypt made Eliakim his brother king over Judah and Jerusalem, and turned his name to Jehoiakim: Pharaoh Neco's renaming of his vassal asserts foreign sovereignty over the Davidic line — both naming and replacing kings (cp. 2 Kgs 23:34). Jehoahaz (Eliakim's brother, deposed in 36:3) is carried off to die in Egypt, fulfilling Jer 22:10-12.

ii-kings|13|22.text: 13:22 The prophecy which Elisha uttered before his death is here followed immediately by the account of its fulfilment, and to this end the oppression of the Israelites by Hazael is mentioned once more, together with that turn of affairs which took place through the compassion of God after the death of Hazael and in the reign of his son Benhadad. לחץ is a pluperfect: "Hazael had oppressed" (for the fact itself compare Kg2 13:4 and Kg2 13:7). For the sake of the covenant made with the patriarchs the Lord turned again to the Israelites, and would not destroy them, and did not cast them away from His face עתּה עד ("till now"), as was the case afterwards, but delivered them from the threatening destruction through the death of Hazael.

ii-kings|19|5.text: 19:5 Isaiah replied with this comforting promise: Hezekiah was not to be afraid of the blasphemous words of the Assyrian king; the Lord would frighten him with a report, so that he would return to his own land, and there would He cause him to fall by the sword. מלך א נערי, the servants or young men of the Assyrian king, is a derogatory epithet applied to the officials of Assyria. "Behold, I put a spirit into him, so that he shall hear a report and return into his own land." שׁמוּעה does not refer to the report of the destruction of his army (Kg2 19:35), as Thenius supposes, for Sennacherib did not hear of this through the medium of an army, but was with the army himself at the time…

ii-samuel|17|29.text: 17:29 in the wilderness—spread out beyond the cultivated tablelands into the steppes of Hauran. Next: 2 Samuel Chapter 18

ii-samuel|22|29.text: 22:29 2 Sam 22:29 commences the description of the help which David had already received from God in his conflict with the enemies of Israel, and which he would still receive. 29 For Thou art my lamp, O Jehovah! And Jehovah maketh my darkness bright. 30 For through Thee I run troops, And through my God I leap walls. 31 God - innocent is His way. The word of Jehovah is refined, A shield is He to all who trust in Him.

ii-samuel|22|30.text: 22:30 In the strength of his God he could run hostile troops and leap walls, i.e., overcome every hostile power. ארוּץ, not from רצץ, to smash in pieces, but from רוּץ, to run; construed with the accusative according to the analogy of verbs of motion.

ii-samuel|22|36.text: 22:36 36 And Thou reachest me the shield of my salvation, And Thy hearing makes me great. 37 Thou makest my steps broad under me, And my ankles have not trembled. The Lord bestows the true strength for victory in His salvation. The shield of salvation is the shield which consists of salvation, of the helping grace of the Lord. ענתך, for which we find in the psalm ענותך, thy humility, i.e., God's condescending grace, does not mean "thy humiliation," but "thy hearkening," i.e., that practical hearkening on the part of God, when called upon for help, which was manifested in the fact that God made his steps broad, i.e., provided the walker with a broad space for free motion, removing obstructions and stumbling-blocks out of the way.

ii-samuel|22|42.text: 22:42 42 They look out, but there is no deliverer; For Jehovah, but He answereth them not. 43 And I rub in pieces as the dust of the earth, Like the mire of the streets I crush them and stamp upon them. The cry of the foe for help is not attended to; they are annihilated without quarter. ישׁעוּ, to look out to God for help (with אל and על; vid., Isa 17:7-8), is more poetical than ישׁוּעוּ, "they cry" (in the psalm);

ii-samuel|22|44.text: 22:44 44 And Thou rescuest me out of the strivings of my people, Preservest me to be the head of the heathen. People that I knew not serve me. 45 The sons of the stranger dissemble to me, Upon hearsay they obey me. 46 The sons of the stranger despair, And tremble out of their castles. By "the strivings of my people" the more indefinite expression in the psalm, "strivings of the people," is explained. The words refer to the domestic conflicts of David, out of which the Lord delivered him, such as the opposition of Ishbosheth and the rebellions of Absalom and Sheba.

ii-samuel|22|47.text: 22:47 47 Jehovah liveth, and blessed is my rock, And the God of my refuge of salvation is exalted. 48 The God who giveth me vengeance, And bringeth nations under me; 49 Who leadeth me out from mine enemies, And exalteth me above mine adversaries, Delivereth me from the man of violence. The formula חי־יהוה does not mean "let Jehovah live," for the word יחי would be used for that (vid., 2 Sam 16:16; 1 Sam 10:24), but is a declaration: "the Lord is living." The declaration itself is to be taken as praise of God, for "praising God is simply ascribing to Him the glorious perfections which belong to him;

ii-samuel|22|50.text: 22:50 50 Therefore will I praise Thee, O Jehovah, among the nations, And sing praise to Thy name. 51 As He who magnifies the salvation of His king, And showeth grace to His anointed, To David, and his seed for ever. The grace which the Lord had shown to David was so great, that the praise thereof could not be restricted to the narrow limits of Israel. With the dominion of David over the nations, there spread also the knowledge, and with this the praise, of the Lord who had given him the victory.

isaiah|7|10.text: 7:10 Here, I. God, by the prophet, makes a gracious offer to Ahaz, to confirm the foregoing predictions, and his faith in them, by such sign or miracle as he should choose (Isa 7:10, Isa 7:11): Ask thee a sign of the Lord thy God; See here the divine faithfulness and veracity. God tells us nothing but what he is able and ready to prove. See his wonderful condescension to the children of men, in that he is so willing to show to the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, Heb 6:17.

job|8|21.text: 8:21 Till—literally, "to the point that"; God's blessing on thee, when repentant, will go on increasing to the point that, or until, &c.

job|16|22.text: 16:22 few—literally, "years of number," that is, few, opposed to numberless (Gen 34:30). Next: Job Chapter 17

joshua|4|15.text: 4:15 Termination of the miraculous Passage through the Jordan. - As soon as the priests left their standing-place in the river with the ark of the covenant, according to the command of God made known to them by Joshua, and the soles of their feet "tore themselves loose upon the dry ground" (נתּקוּ אל החרבה, constructio praegnans, for they tore themselves loose from the soft soil of the river, and trode upon the dry or firm ground), the waters of the Jordan returned again to their place, and went over all its banks as before (vid., Jos 3:15).

leviticus|21|24.text: 21:24 Moses told it unto Aaron, and to his sons, and unto all the children of Israel: The closing transmission-formula for the priestly holiness code (ch. 21). The chain of communication — Lord to Moses to Aaron to the priests to the people — secures the regulations within the covenant community. Holiness was not esoteric; the whole congregation heard the priests' calling.

leviticus|23|33.text: 23:33 We have here, I. The institution of the feast of tabernacles, which was one of the three great feasts at which all the males were bound to attend, and celebrated with more expressions of joy than any of them. 1. As to the directions for regulating this feast, observe, (1.) It was to be observed on the fifteenth day of the seventh month (Lev 23:34), but five days after the day of atonement. We may suppose, though they were not all bound to attend on the day of atonement, as on the three great festivals, yet that many of the devout Jews came up so many days before the feast of tabernacles as to enjoy the opportunity of attending on the day of atonement.

nehemiah|11|26.text: 11:26 At Jeshua, and at Moladah, and at Beth-phelet: Three southern towns repopulated by Judahites. *Yeshua* (also Joshua) is otherwise unattested as a Judahite settlement; the name may commemorate the local figure or simply mean salvation. *Moladah* and *Beth-phelet* appear in Joshua's southern allotment (Josh 15:26-27), recovered after exile.

nehemiah|11|28.text: 11:28 At Ziklag, and at Mekonah, and in the villages thereof: Ziklag — David's haven during Saul's pursuit (1 Sam 27:6) and the city of the Amalekite raid (1 Sam 30) — is restored to Judah. *Mekonah* is not securely identified; its inclusion preserves a regional resettlement claim more than a recognizable city.

nehemiah|11|31.text: 11:31 The children also of Benjamin from Geba dwelt at Michmash, and Aija, and Beth-el: The Benjaminite resettlement spread north of Jerusalem along the old central spine. *Geba*, *Michmash*, and *Beth-el* were Saul-era strongholds (1 Sam 13:2; 14:5) and centers of Israelite memory — places where Judges and Samuel had named God's earlier dealings with his people.

nehemiah|11|32.text: 11:32 At Anathoth, Nob, Ananiah: Three more Benjaminite settlements north of Jerusalem. *Anathoth* — Jeremiah's hometown (Jer 1:1) — was a priestly city (Josh 21:18). *Nob* — destroyed by Saul (1 Sam 22:19) — is restored. Geography itself was repaired by the return; ancient towns reclaimed their names.

nehemiah|11|33.text: 11:33 Hadid - This place is also unknown. Neballat - Also unknown.

numbers|13|31.text: 13:31 But his companions were of an opposite opinion, and declared that the people in Canaan were stronger than the Israelites, and therefore it was impossible to go up to it.

numbers|26|28.text: 26:28 And the Lord spake unto Moses,.... After the sum of the people of Israel had been taken: saying; as follows.

numbers|29|40.text: 29:40 Num 29:40 forms the conclusion of the list of sacrifices in ch. 28 and 29.

proverbs|26|28.text: 26:28 There are two sorts of lies equally detestable: - 1. A slandering lie, which avowedly hates those it is spoken of: A lying tongue hates those that are afflicted by it; it afflicts them by calumnies and reproaches because it hates them, and can thus smite them secretly where they are without defence; and it hates them because it has afflicted them and made them its enemies. The mischief of this is open and obvious; it afflicts, it hates, and owns it, and every body sees it.

psalms|34|22.text: 34:22 (Heb.: 34:23) The order of the alphabet having been gone through, there now follows a second פ exactly like Ps 25:22. Just as the first פ, Ps 25:16, is פּנה, so here in Ps 34:17 it is פּני; and in like manner the two supernumerary Phe's correspond to one another - the Elohimic in the former Psalm, and the Jehovic in this latter.

zechariah|7|13.text: 7:13 This wrath is described in Zac 7:13, Zac 7:14. Zac 7:13. "It came to pass: as he cried and they did not hear, so will they cry and I shall not hear, said Jehovah of hosts. Zac 7:14. And I will scatter them with a whirlwind over all nations, who did not know them, and the land is laid waste behind them, so that no one passes to and fro. And thus they made the choice land a desert." The form of the address changes in Zac 7:13.

daniel|4|21.text: 4:21 Whose leaves were fair, and the fruit thereof much: The tree's universal provision — shelter for beasts, nesting for birds, food for all — pictures Nebuchadnezzar's imperial reach over conquered peoples (cp. Ezek 31:6; Dan 2:38). The grand image is the prelude to its felling, a warning that dominion held in pride invites divine humbling (4:25, 30-31).

deuteronomy|5|13.text: 5:13 Six days thou shalt labour: The Sabbath command frames work itself as gift, not curse. The six-day pattern echoes God's own creative week (Gen 1:31–2:3) and dignifies labor as a divine ordinance — not merely a precondition for rest but the field in which faithfulness is daily proved (cp. Eph 4:28).

deuteronomy|5|19.text: 5:19 Neither shalt thou steal: The eighth commandment protects the neighbor's livelihood and the social trust on which covenant life depends. The Hebrew verb *ganav* covers theft, kidnapping, and economic deceit (see Exod 21:16; Lev 19:11, 13). Jesus retains the command in his summary of the law (Matt 19:18; cp. Eph 4:28).

deuteronomy|5|20.text: 5:20 Neither shalt thou bear false witness: The ninth commandment guards the integrity of the courtroom and the wider community against malicious testimony. *Shav* (false, vain) widens the reach beyond formal perjury to slander and rumor (cp. Exod 23:1; Prov 19:5; Eph 4:25). Truthful speech is the soil in which justice can grow.

deuteronomy|5|30.text: 5:30 Get you into your tents again: After the people's terror at Sinai (5:23-27), the Lord dismisses Israel and retains only Moses as mediator. The command marks a turning point — the people themselves request mediated revelation (cp. Heb 12:18-21), and the office of prophet (Deut 18:15-19) takes form.

deuteronomy|5|31.text: 5:31 But as for thee, stand thou here by me: Moses' unique role as covenant mediator is sealed. He alone receives the commandments, statutes, and judgments to teach Israel (cp. Exod 20:21; John 1:17). The verse anticipates the prophet-like-Moses promise (Deut 18:18) fulfilled in Christ (Acts 3:22).

deuteronomy|5|32.text: 5:32 Ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left: A standing formula in Deuteronomy for unwavering covenant obedience (see 17:11, 20; 28:14; Josh 1:7). The path of life is narrow; faithfulness is measured not by intention but by steady walking in the commanded way (cp. Prov 4:27; Matt 7:14).

deuteronomy|8|20.text: 8:20 As the nations which the Lord destroyeth: The covenant cuts both ways. Israel's tenure in the land is not racial inheritance but conditional gift; the same Lord who removed the Canaanites for disobedience will, if Israel imitates them, remove Israel (cp. Lev 18:24-28; 2 Kgs 17:7-23). Election does not exempt from accountability.

deuteronomy|9|28.text: 9:28 Lest the land whence thou broughtest us out say: Moses' intercession appeals to God's reputation among the nations. Were Israel destroyed in the wilderness, Egypt would conclude that the Lord lacked power or willingness — a slander Moses cannot tolerate (cp. Exod 32:12; Num 14:13-16; Ezek 36:22).

deuteronomy|9|29.text: 9:29 Yet they are thy people and thine inheritance: Moses closes his intercession by appealing to election, not merit. Israel belongs to the Lord not because of righteousness but because he chose them and brought them out *bekoach gadol* — with great power (cp. Exod 6:6-7; Deut 7:7-8; Eph 1:11).

deuteronomy|11|19.text: 11:19 Ye shall teach them your children: The law is to saturate ordinary life — at table, on the road, at bedtime, at waking. The formula extends 6:7 and becomes the rhythm of Israelite catechesis. Deuteronomy assumes that covenant survives only when each generation hears the words afresh (cp. Ps 78:5-7; Eph 6:4).

deuteronomy|11|20.text: 11:20 Thou shalt write them upon the door posts: The companion command to 11:19 — visual catechesis to accompany verbal. The *mezuzah* tradition derives from this verse and from 6:9, the words of God marking thresholds as one enters or leaves. Faithfulness is to be public, not private, and recurring, not occasional.

deuteronomy|11|31.text: 11:31 For ye shall pass over Jordan: The exhortation looks past Moses' own life to the imminent conquest under Joshua. The land is gift and inheritance — *nahalah* — given by God's promise to the patriarchs (cp. Gen 12:7; Deut 1:8; Heb 11:9). Possession will require obedience to keep.

deuteronomy|11|32.text: 11:32 Ye shall observe to do all the statutes: The transition formula closing the sermon and introducing the law-code of chs 12–26. The summons is comprehensive — not selective obedience but every statute and judgment, every commandment kept as a single woven cloth (cp. Jas 2:10).

deuteronomy|14|10.text: 14:10 Whatsoever hath not fins and scales: The dietary law for aquatic creatures simplifies to a visible test, just as the rules for land animals reduced to cloven hoof and chewed cud (14:6). The criterion may reflect anatomical normality within a habitat; theologically, the distinctions train Israel in discrimination — holiness as practiced perception (Lev 11:9-12).

deuteronomy|14|29.text: 14:29 The Levite, and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow: The triennial tithe redistributes covenant abundance to those without inherited land. The fourfold list — repeated in 26:12-13 — names the structurally vulnerable. The blessing-clause binds Israel's prosperity to its generosity (cp. Prov 19:17; Matt 25:40).

deuteronomy|19|20.text: 19:20 Those which remain shall hear, and fear: The deterrent function of judicial penalty. The Hebrew pairing *shama* (hear) and *yare* (fear) recurs in Deuteronomy's discipline laws (see 13:11; 17:13; 21:21). Public justice teaches the community what kind of evil cannot be tolerated and shapes communal reverence.

deuteronomy|28|65.text: 28:65 Among these nations shalt thou find no ease: The exile-curse intensifies — physical wandering joined to inner unrest. *Margo'a* (rest) is denied even to the foot's sole. The body's exhaustion mirrors the soul's: a trembling heart, failing eyes, sorrow of mind (cp. Lev 26:36; Jer 9:16; Lam 1:3).

deuteronomy|28|66.text: 28:66 Thy life shall hang in doubt before thee: The covenant curse touches the deepest layer of human existence — the sense that life itself is uncertain. *Talui* (hanging) figures a life suspended, neither secured nor surrendered. The dread haunts day and night, anticipating the loss of all assurance that obedience would have guaranteed (cp. Lev 26:36).

deuteronomy|28|67.text: 28:67 In the morning thou shalt say, Would God it were even: The curse's psychological climax — time itself becomes torment. Each watch of day and night is wished away. Such despair, foreseen 800 years before the exiles drank it, is named in Lamentations (3:17-18) and recurs in Israel's prophetic literature (cp. Job 7:4; Rev 9:6).

esther|8|16.text: 8:16 The Jews had light, and gladness, and joy, and honour: The four-fold cluster names the inversion that defines the book — what was a decree of annihilation (3:13) becomes festal joy. *Or* (light) often pairs with deliverance in Hebrew (Ps 27:1; 97:11), and the reversal foreshadows the annual feast of Purim (9:20-22).

exodus|6|27.text: 6:27 These are that Moses and Aaron: The narrator interrupts the genealogy (6:14-25) to anchor the brothers within the Levitical line, then resumes the deliverance story. The aside legitimates Aaron's later priesthood as well as Moses' prophetic role, the priesthood and prophecy descending from the same parental house (cp. Num 26:59).

exodus|6|29.text: 6:29 I am the Lord: speak thou unto Pharaoh: The Lord's self-disclosure reopens the commissioning interrupted by genealogy. The covenant name *YHWH* grounds the command: it is the same God of Sinai and the patriarchs who now sends Moses to confront Egypt's king (cp. 3:14; 6:2-8).

exodus|6|30.text: 6:30 I am of uncircumcised lips: Moses returns to his earlier objection (4:10), naming himself *aral sephatayim* — lips outside the covenant of fluent speech. The image draws on circumcision's wider Hebrew use for openness to God's purpose. Pharaoh's hearing is not Moses' problem to solve; the Lord supplies Aaron (4:14-16).

exodus|34|34.text: 34:34 He took the vail off, until he came out: The pattern formalizes Moses' mediatorial office. Unveiled before the Lord, veiled before Israel — the rhythm communicates that the glory cannot yet be borne directly. Paul takes up the image in 2 Cor 3:13-18 as the figure of the new-covenant face turned to behold the Lord with open countenance.

exodus|34|35.text: 34:35 The children of Israel saw the face of Moses: The radiance is *qaran* — to shine, to send out beams. The visible glory tells Israel that revelation has been received in Moses' favor. The veil is not deception but mercy, masking what would otherwise overwhelm (cp. 2 Cor 3:7), until the same glory shines fully in Christ (2 Cor 4:6).

exodus|38|12.text: 38:12 For the west side were hangings of fifty cubits: The tabernacle court's western boundary completes the rectangle (50×100 cubits). The careful counting of pillars (ten) and silver fittings underlines the precision the Lord required. No detail of the sanctuary was left to improvisation — it was patterned after the heavenly original (cp. 25:9; Heb 8:5).

exodus|38|13.text: 38:13 For the east side eastward fifty cubits: The eastern boundary, fronting the rising sun, faced Israel's approach to worship. Throughout Scripture the east entrance carries weight: the cherubim guard the way from the east (Gen 3:24); Ezekiel sees the glory return from the east (Ezek 43:1-4).

exodus|38|14.text: 38:14 The hangings of the one side of the gate were fifteen cubits: The gate's southern flank, with three pillars and three sockets, holds the curtain that frames the entrance. The proportions (15 + 20 + 15 = 50 cubits across the east face) preserve a measured symmetry that befits the tabernacle's purpose as model of cosmic order (cp. 25:40).

exodus|38|15.text: 38:15 For the other side of the court gate: The northern flank mirrors the southern (38:14), confirming the gate's twenty-cubit central span. The mirrored measurements were not architectural ornament but spiritual instruction: the way into God's presence is balanced, intentional, and precisely as the Lord prescribed (cp. Heb 9:6-7).

exodus|38|16.text: 38:16 All the hangings of the court round about were of fine twined linen: *Shesh moshzar* — six-stranded white linen — encloses the entire courtyard. The white wall set apart sacred ground from common space, visible from a distance as Israel encamped tribally around the tabernacle. White figures the holiness that frames God's dwelling (cp. Lev 16:4; Rev 19:8).

exodus|38|19.text: 38:19 Their pillars were four, and their sockets of brass four: The gate proper — twenty cubits wide — rested on four bronze sockets supporting four pillars draped with the embroidered curtain (38:18). Bronze marks the courtyard's outer ring; silver and gold belong to the inner sanctities. The metallic gradation traces a topography of holiness (cp. Heb 9:1-5).

exodus|38|20.text: 38:20 All the pins of the tabernacle were of brass: Tent pegs were not afterthoughts. Bronze pins anchored the courtyard's linen wall and the tabernacle's covering, binding the sanctuary to the earth itself. Even the most humble fixture was named, counted, and consecrated — no part of the dwelling was outside the Lord's reckoning (cp. 27:19).

exodus|38|30.text: 38:30 Therewith he made the sockets to the door of the tabernacle: Bezalel's bronze inventory includes door sockets, the great altar, its grate, and all altar vessels. The materials donated by the people (38:29) become the very furniture of worship — gift transformed into ministry (cp. 1 Chr 29:14; 1 Cor 12:5).

exodus|38|31.text: 38:31 Sockets of the court round about, and of the court gate, and all the pins: The closing inventory completes the tally. Every bronze item is accounted for; every contribution from Israel finds its place in the sanctuary. The exhaustive enumeration testifies that the tabernacle was built with full integrity, the people's gifts neither lost nor diverted.

exodus|39|31.text: 39:31 They tied unto it a lace of blue: *Pethil tekheleth* — the blue cord — fastens the gold plate engraved Holy to the Lord (28:36-37) to Aaron's turban. Blue throughout the priestly garments signals heaven's authority resting on the head of Israel's mediator. The phrase as the Lord commanded Moses recurs as the chapter's refrain of exact obedience (cp. 39:1, 5, 7, 21).

ezekiel|41|26.text: 41:26 Narrow windows and palm trees on the one side and on the other: The porch ornamentation of Ezekiel's visionary temple bears the palm motif first seen in Solomon's house (1 Kgs 6:29-32). *Tamar* (palm) signified righteousness and flourishing (Ps 92:12) and adorned the new temple as it had the old, signaling continuity between former glory and the dwelling yet to come.

ezra|2|67.text: 2:67 Their camels, four hundred thirty and five; their asses, six thousand seven hundred and twenty: The animal census closes the register of returnees (2:64-67). The sheer volume of livestock signals a serious resettlement effort, not a token return. Camels, rare in earlier Israelite lists, point to the prosperity some exiles carried back from Persia.

ezra|10|20.text: 10:20 Of the sons of Immer; Hanani, and Zebadiah: The roll of priests who married foreign wives opens with the house of Immer. That the priesthood itself stood among the offenders intensifies the crisis — Ezra's reform spared no caste (cp. Ezra 9:1-2; Neh 13:28). Restoration required confession from the leaders before the people could follow.

ezra|10|21.text: 10:21 Of the sons of Harim; Maaseiah, and Elijah, and Shemaiah, and Jehiel, and Uzziah: A second priestly house enrolled among those who put away foreign wives. Harim is also listed at the return (Ezra 2:39) and among signatories of the covenant renewal (Neh 10:5). Repentance, not lineage, restored their priestly standing.

ezra|10|22.text: 10:22 Of the sons of Pashur: A third priestly clan (Ezra 2:38) named in the reform. Pashur's descendants would later sign Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:3), suggesting that the discipline of Ezra 10 did not break the priesthood but purified it. Repentance preserved continuity of office.

ezra|10|26.text: 10:26 Of the sons of Elam: The list shifts from priests (10:18-22) to lay Israelites; Elam was among the larger returnee families (Ezra 2:7). The transition shows that the reform reached every stratum — the same standard of covenant fidelity applied to priest and layman alike.

ezra|10|27.text: 10:27 Of the sons of Zattu: Another large lay family (Ezra 2:8) named among those who repented of mixed marriage. The repetition of family-name + sons-by-name preserves accountability — neither anonymous penance nor blanket absolution, but each man named before the community.

ezra|10|28.text: 10:28 Of the sons also of Bebai: A smaller clan (Ezra 2:11; eight names total). The thoroughness of the list — sometimes only four or five men per family — testifies both to the limited reach of the offense and to the precision of the reform.

ezra|10|29.text: 10:29 Of the sons of Bani: Six men from one of the substantial returnee houses (Ezra 2:10). The Bani clan reappears repeatedly in the list (10:34, 38), suggesting the family had spread out and intermarried widely.

ezra|10|30.text: 10:30 Of the sons of Pahath-moab: The largest single-family entry in the chapter (eight men), matching Pahath-moab's prominence at the return (Ezra 2:6 — 2,812 souls). Larger families faced proportional accountability; size offered no shelter.

ezra|10|31.text: 10:31 Of the sons of Harim: A lay branch of Harim, distinct from the priestly Harim of 10:21. The doubled occurrence within a single chapter shows how widespread foreign marriage had become — touching both pulpit and pew of the post-exilic community.

ezra|10|32.text: 10:32 Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah: The continuation of the Harim list (10:31). Splitting the entry across verses preserves the original document's pacing; the Chronicler-style register is faithfully reproduced from Ezra's own scribal records.

ezra|10|33.text: 10:33 Of the sons of Hashum: Hashum's family appears in earlier registers (Ezra 2:19) and at the covenant renewal (Neh 10:18). Seven men named here suggest the family bore notable involvement in the offense — and notable willingness to remedy it.

ezra|10|34.text: 10:34 Of the sons of Bani: A second listing of Bani's offenders (cp. 10:29). The Bani name spans more than ten verses in the register (10:34-42), pointing either to multiple branches sharing a name or to one very large family widely tangled in mixed marriage.

ezra|10|35.text: 10:35 Benaiah, Bedeiah, Chelluh: The Bani list continues. The names — many bearing *El* or *Yah* compounds (Benaiah, 'YHWH has built') — show that men of Yahwistic households had still drifted into prohibited unions. Pious upbringing did not immunize against compromise.

ezra|10|36.text: 10:36 Vaniah, Meremoth, Eliashib: A name like Eliashib (compare the high priest of Neh 3:1) appears here as an offender, again confirming that the reform reached deep into prominent households. Common names complicate identification, but the principle stands: status did not exempt.

ezra|10|37.text: 10:37 Mattaniah, Mattenai, and Jaasau: The Bani list continues without commentary. The bare register-style mirrors the Babylonian and Persian administrative documents Ezra would have known, lending the reform record official weight.

ezra|10|38.text: 10:38 And Bani, and Binnui, Shimei: A man named Bani appears within the Bani list itself — a son named after the patriarch, common in extended Israelite families. The register's literal repetition resists tidy reorganization, preserving each man's name.

ezra|10|39.text: 10:39 And Shelemiah, and Nathan, and Adaiah: Three more names continue the Bani roll. The reform was costly: each man named here renounced wife and (often) children (cp. 10:3, 44). The pain of these severings makes the bare list of names a record of grief as well as obedience.

ezra|10|40.text: 10:40 Machnadebai, Shashai, Sharai: Names of uncertain meaning — Machnadebai may be Persian in origin, hinting that exile-era families had absorbed foreign cultural markers even in their naming practices. The reform sought to recover covenant identity at every level.

ezra|10|41.text: 10:41 Azareel, and Shelemiah, Shemariah: The list nears completion. Yahwistic names dominate (Azareel — 'God has helped'; Shemariah — 'YHWH has guarded'), reminding the reader that the offenders were not pagan but covenant Israelites who had departed from the law (Deut 7:3).

ezra|10|42.text: 10:42 Shallum, Amariah, and Joseph: The Bani register closes. The last name Joseph echoes the patriarch and recalls Israel's long history of preserved identity in foreign lands — a memory the reform now reactivates for the post-exilic generation.

ezra|10|43.text: 10:43 Of the sons of Nebo: The final family in the chapter — Nebo, a smaller clan (Ezra 2:29; Neh 7:33). The verse concludes the personnel roster; verse 44 supplies the brief summary of the wives and children put away, closing the book on a costly act of obedience.

genesis|5|30.text: 5:30 Lamech lived after he begat Noah five hundred ninety and five years: The patriarch's post-Noah lifespan extends the antediluvian chronology toward the flood. Lamech's earlier prophecy that Noah would bring rest (5:29) hangs over these long years — a hope deferred but not extinguished, awaiting the deluge generation (Gen 6:5-8).

genesis|5|31.text: 5:31 All the days of Lamech were seven hundred seventy and seven years: Lamech's total — 777 years — closes a life of striking numeric symmetry. Whether the number is symbolic of completion or simply preserved from a longer tradition, Lamech dies before the flood, sparing the patriarch the sight of judgment (cp. 2 Kgs 22:20; Isa 57:1).

genesis|7|23.text: 7:23 Noah only remained alive, and they that were with him: The covenant-clause of preservation. Where verse 22 names what was destroyed, verse 23 names what remained — a single household with the living cargo of the ark. The verb *sha'ar* (remained) anticipates the doctrine of remnant that runs through Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Paul (Isa 10:21; Rom 11:5).

genesis|11|32.text: 11:32 The days of Terah were two hundred and five years: Terah's death at Haran closes the prologue to Abraham's call. Stephen reads this verse as marking the moment Abraham left Haran for Canaan (Acts 7:4), though the narrative ordering in Genesis is theological rather than strictly chronological. Terah's pilgrimage was incomplete; his son's would not be.

genesis|15|21.text: 15:21 The Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Girgashites, and the Jebusites: The land-grant of 15:18-21 closes with four peoples completing a tenfold list. The boundaries described — Egypt's river to the Euphrates — exceed Israel's actual possession at any historical moment, pointing to a fullness yet to come (cp. Heb 11:39-40).

genesis|24|66.text: 24:66 The servant told Isaac all things that he had done: The faithful servant — unnamed throughout the chapter, by tradition Eliezer of 15:2 — renders his account before the bride is given. The pattern of the trusted servant who succeeds because he trusts the Lord recurs in Scripture (cp. 24:12-14, 27; Matt 25:21).

genesis|46|32.text: 46:32 The men are shepherds, for their trade hath been to feed cattle: Joseph coaches his brothers' answer to Pharaoh. *Roe tsoan* (keeper of flocks) was abominable to Egyptians (46:34), and Joseph turns the cultural stigma to his family's advantage — they will be granted Goshen, a region apart, which preserves their distinct identity through the generations of growth (Exod 1:7).

genesis|46|33.text: 46:33 When Pharaoh shall call you, and shall say, What is your occupation?: Joseph anticipates the inevitable royal interview. The detail shows Joseph's wisdom for diaspora life — preparing his family to speak truthfully and shrewdly within a foreign court (cp. Dan 1:8; Esth 4:14). Pharaoh's question is the gate; their answer the key to Goshen.

i-chronicles|1|15.text: 1:15 The Hivite, and the Arkite, and the Sinite: Three of the seven Canaanite peoples descended from Canaan (1:13-16; cp. Gen 10:15-18). The Chronicler lists them to root post-exilic Israel's claim to the land in the table of nations — the same peoples whose dispossession Joshua records (Josh 24:11).

i-chronicles|1|16.text: 1:16 The Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite: The closing trio of Canaanite peoples stretches the genealogy north into Phoenicia. Arvad and Hamath remained major Aramean centers into the prophets' day (cp. Ezek 27:8, 11; Amos 6:2), framing Canaan's full geographic reach in the inherited promise.

i-chronicles|1|21.text: 1:21 Hadoram also, and Uzal, and Diklah: Three of the thirteen sons of Joktan (1:19-23), peopling southern Arabia. Uzal is linked to Sana (modern Yemen); Hadoram and Diklah are likewise Arabian. The Chronicler traces the Semitic peoples beyond Israel to show the wider human family from which Abraham was called (cp. Gen 10:26-29).

i-chronicles|2|36.text: 2:36 Attai begat Nathan, and Nathan begat Zabad: One link of the Jerahmeelite line through Sheshan (2:34-35). The genealogy preserves the line of an Egyptian servant adopted to perpetuate Sheshan's name when sons failed — an early biblical case of inheritance by adoption (cp. Eph 1:5).

i-chronicles|2|37.text: 2:37 Zabad begat Ephlal, and Ephlal begat Obed: The Jerahmeelite chain continues. *Obed* (servant) is a recurring covenant name in the Davidic line as well (cp. Ruth 4:21-22), though this Obed belongs to a separate branch of Judah's tribe.

i-chronicles|2|38.text: 2:38 Obed begat Jehu, and Jehu begat Azariah: Names common in later Israelite history attach to ordinary men in this register. Jehu here is not the king of Israel (2 Kgs 9–10) but a Judahite of obscure standing — a reminder that the Chronicler's roll honors faithful continuity, not famous achievement.

i-chronicles|2|39.text: 2:39 Azariah begat Helez, and Helez begat Eleasah: Six generations into the Jerahmeelite branch. The slow, generation-by-generation enumeration is its own kind of theology: covenant faithfulness measured not in single great events but in steady transmission across centuries.

i-chronicles|2|40.text: 2:40 Eleasah begat Sisamai, and Sisamai begat Shallum: Names of uncertain etymology, possibly preserving traces of the Egyptian ancestry mentioned in 2:34-35. The continuity of the line through cultural mixing testifies that covenant identity could absorb without dissolving (cp. Ruth 4:13-17).

i-chronicles|2|41.text: 2:41 Shallum begat Jekamiah, and Jekamiah begat Elishama: The Jerahmeelite line closes with Elishama — possibly the official mentioned in 2 Kgs 25:25 or Jer 41:1. If so, the line bore service into the very end of the kingdom of Judah, finally meeting the exile that Chronicles writes after.

i-chronicles|2|49.text: 2:49 She bare also Shaaph the father of Madmannah: Caleb's concubine Maachah (2:48) produced a line tied to specific south-Judah towns — Madmannah, Machbenah, Gibea. Personal genealogy and town-founding overlap freely in early Israelite memory; an ancestor's name often denoted the place his clan settled.

i-chronicles|2|50.text: 2:50 These were the sons of Caleb the son of Hur: The Calebite line of Hur (not the Caleb son of Jephunneh of the spies; cp. Num 13:6). Shobal — father of Kiriath-jearim — places the family in the territory north of Hebron, including the town that long sheltered the ark (1 Sam 7:1).

i-chronicles|2|51.text: 2:51 Salma the father of Beth-lehem, Hareph the father of Beth-gader: Two more Calebite settlements. Bethlehem here is named for an ancestor who founded or fathered the town — the same Bethlehem that would receive Boaz, Ruth, David, and ultimately the Messiah (Mic 5:2; Matt 2:1).

i-chronicles|3|23.text: 3:23 The sons of Neariah; Elioenai, and Hezekiah, and Azrikam, three: The genealogy of David's line continues five generations past Zerubbabel (3:19) into the post-exilic period. Hezekiah here is not the king but a namesake — the Chronicler keeps the Davidic family alive in the reader's memory across the long silence between Malachi and Matthew.

i-chronicles|4|42.text: 4:42 Some of them, even of the sons of Simeon, five hundred men, went to mount Seir: A Simeonite expedition into Edomite territory during Hezekiah's reign (4:41), led by four captains. The note preserves a fragment of tribal history showing that Simeon — though absorbed into Judah — still acted as a recognizable unit centuries after the conquest.

i-chronicles|6|11.text: 6:11 Azariah begat Amariah, and Amariah begat Ahitub: A central link in the Aaronic high-priestly succession. Ahitub will father Zadok (6:12), the priest who served David and Solomon and whose line would dominate the post-exilic priesthood (cp. 2 Sam 8:17; Ezek 44:15).

i-chronicles|6|12.text: 6:12 Ahitub begat Zadok, and Zadok begat Shallum: Zadok's loyalty to David secured his line's permanent place in the priesthood. The Chronicler traces it forward through Shallum, anchoring the post-exilic priesthood in the Davidic-Solomonic origin (cp. 1 Kgs 1:8, 39; 2:35).

i-chronicles|6|13.text: 6:13 Shallum begat Hilkiah, and Hilkiah begat Azariah: Hilkiah is most likely the high priest who discovered the Book of the Law during Josiah's renovation of the temple (2 Kgs 22:8), the act that sparked the reform of 622 BC. The line moves from Davidic origin toward the brink of exile.

i-chronicles|6|15.text: 6:15 Jehozadak went into captivity, when the Lord carried away Judah: The high-priestly line meets the exile. Jehozadak's son Jeshua will return with Zerubbabel to lead the rebuilt altar's first sacrifices (Ezra 3:2; Hag 1:1). The priesthood survives the breach, carrying covenant continuity through the rupture.

i-chronicles|6|30.text: 6:30 Shimea his son, Haggiah his son, Asaiah his son: Three generations of the Merarite line, the Levitical branch responsible for the tabernacle's frames and bases (Num 3:36-37). Their service was structural rather than ceremonial — quiet, indispensable work in the economy of worship.

i-chronicles|6|34.text: 6:34 The son of Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Eliel, the son of Toah: Four ascending generations toward Heman (6:33), David's chief singer. The reverse-order genealogy traces the family back from Heman to Levi (cp. 6:38), establishing the Levitical credential for temple song.

i-chronicles|6|35.text: 6:35 The son of Zuph, the son of Elkanah, the son of Mahath, the son of Amasai: Continuing Heman's ascending line. *Zuph* connects this family to the territory of Zuphim, where Saul searched for his lost donkeys and encountered Samuel (1 Sam 9:5) — the Levitical singer Heman and the prophet Samuel share an ancestral district.

i-chronicles|6|36.text: 6:36 The son of Elkanah, the son of Joel, the son of Azariah, the son of Zephaniah: Four more generations. The name *Elkanah* recurs in the line — by tradition Hannah's husband (1 Sam 1:1) belongs to this very family, making Heman the singer a descendant of the prophet Samuel.

i-chronicles|6|37.text: 6:37 The son of Tahath, the son of Assir, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah: The line ascends to Korah, leader of the rebellion against Moses (Num 16). That the Korahites later became one of the great families of temple song (cp. Pss 42–49 titles) shows judgment did not annul mercy — Korah's grandchildren served at the altar.

i-chronicles|6|38.text: 6:38 The son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi, the son of Israel: The ascending genealogy reaches its summit — Levi son of Israel. Heman the singer (6:33) is grafted into the patriarchal line through fifteen generations, his ministry of song a Levitical inheritance reaching back to Sinai itself.

i-chronicles|6|40.text: 6:40 The son of Michael, the son of Baaseiah, the son of Malchiah: A second singer-line, that of Asaph (6:39), is now traced. Asaph's psalms (Pss 50, 73–83) bore his name into later worship; the genealogy here legitimates his standing in the Levitical brotherhood.

i-chronicles|6|41.text: 6:41 The son of Ethni, the son of Zerah, the son of Adaiah: Continued ascent in Asaph's line. The names — most appearing nowhere else in Scripture — are preserved not for narrative interest but for priestly registry: covenant memory does not forget the obscure servants.

i-chronicles|6|43.text: 6:43 The son of Jahath, the son of Gershom, the son of Levi: Asaph's line reaches Gershom, eldest son of Levi (cp. 23:7). Where Heman traced through Kohath (6:38), Asaph traces through Gershom — the temple choir drew from multiple Levitical houses, the music of worship a genuinely shared inheritance.

i-chronicles|6|45.text: 6:45 The son of Hashabiah, the son of Amaziah, the son of Hilkiah: The third singer-line, that of Ethan the Merarite (6:44), is now traced. Three families — Heman, Asaph, Ethan — together led David's musical service (cp. 15:17, 19), each grounded in one of Levi's three principal houses.

i-chronicles|6|46.text: 6:46 The son of Amzi, the son of Bani, the son of Shamer: Ethan's line ascends through more generations. The triple-line structure of the singers (Heman-Asaph-Ethan) modeled the unity of Levi's tribe in worship — three families, three branches, one ministry.

i-chronicles|6|47.text: 6:47 The son of Mahli, the son of Mushi, the son of Merari, the son of Levi: Ethan's line reaches Merari, Levi's third son. The three great singer-genealogies (Heman through Kohath, Asaph through Gershom, Ethan through Merari) together gather all of Levi into the temple's worship — no branch excluded from praise.

i-chronicles|7|26.text: 7:26 Laadan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son: The Ephraimite line that produced Joshua (7:27). Ammihud and Elishama are named as Joshua's grandfather and father; in Num 1:10 Elishama is chief of Ephraim's host at the second-year census, supplying the leader at the conquest.

i-chronicles|7|27.text: 7:27 Non his son, Jehoshua his son: *Jehoshua* (Joshua) — the Ephraimite who succeeded Moses and led the conquest — descends from a deliberately recorded line. The Chronicler closes the Ephraimite genealogy with Joshua, whose name signifies *YHWH saves* and looks forward to a greater Jeshua (Matt 1:21).

i-chronicles|7|31.text: 7:31 The sons of Beriah; Heber, and Malchiel, who is the father of Birzavith: The line of Asher continues. Malchiel founded Birzavith, an Asherite town; Heber would father Japhlet (7:32), whose descendants populate verses 33-34. The Chronicler tracks Asher's territorial roots in western Galilee.

i-chronicles|7|33.text: 7:33 The sons of Japhlet; Pasach, and Bimhal, and Ashvath: Three more Asherite names. Japhlet appears outside this genealogy only in Josh 16:3, naming a border town in Ephraim — the same family may have spread to Ephraimite territory, reflecting tribal intermingling along Israel's central spine.

i-chronicles|7|34.text: 7:34 The sons of Shamer; Ahi, and Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram: A second Asherite branch. *Aram* here is a personal name within Asher, not the northern kingdom — common-name collisions are typical in tribal lists and remind the reader that genealogy was lived as ordinary family memory.

i-chronicles|7|35.text: 7:35 The sons of his brother Helem; Zophah, and Imna, and Shelesh, and Amal: Helem's branch parallels Shamer's. The Asherite list grows by careful subdivision — each grandson named, each clan branch identified — preserving the territorial claims that mattered for inheritance and military census.

i-chronicles|7|36.text: 7:36 The sons of Zophah; Suah, and Harnepher, and Shual, and Beri, and Imrah: Zophah's six sons (continuing into 7:37) make him the most prolific branch in this section of Asher. The genealogy reads almost as a tribal directory — names that meant little to outsiders meant everything to the families they identified.

i-chronicles|7|37.text: 7:37 Bezer, and Hod, and Shamma, and Shilshah, and Ithran, and Beera: Six more sons of Zophah. The eleven-name list (7:36-37) is unusually long, suggesting Zophah's clan held disproportionate weight in Asher's federation — a memory of relative tribal influence preserved in the Chronicler's roll.

i-chronicles|7|38.text: 7:38 The sons of Jether; Jephunneh, and Pispah, and Ara: A smaller Asherite line. The same name *Jephunneh* belonged to Caleb's father (Num 13:6), but tribal name-sharing is common; this Jephunneh is firmly within Asher's borders.

i-chronicles|7|39.text: 7:39 The sons of Ulla; Arah, and Haniel, and Rezia: The Asherite catalog closes. *Haniel* (favor of God) was also the name of an Asherite chief at the second-year census (Num 34:23); whether the same person or a namesake, the recurrence shows Asher's families preserving their distinctive names across generations.

i-chronicles|8|5.text: 8:5 Gera, and Shephuphan, and Huram: Three sons of Bela, son of Benjamin. The Benjaminite line will run toward Saul (8:33) and beyond, threading the tribe of the first king through a careful register. *Gera* will reappear in Saul's family as the father of Shimei (2 Sam 16:5).

i-chronicles|8|11.text: 8:11 Of Hushim he begat Abitub, and Elpaal: A line of Benjamin's eastern branch. Elpaal's many sons fill the surrounding verses (8:12, 17-18), making him an unusually prolific patriarch within Benjamin and signaling the tribe's continued vitality even after its near-extinction in Judg 20–21.

i-chronicles|8|16.text: 8:16 Michael, and Ispah, and Joha, the sons of Beriah: A second Beriah within Benjamin (cp. 7:23, 30 for Beriahs in other tribes). The name — meaning 'in calamity' — was given in commemoration of family suffering and reflects how Israelite naming embedded memory in identity.

i-chronicles|8|18.text: 8:18 Ishmerai also, and Jezliah, and Jobab, the sons of Elpaal: Three more sons of Elpaal (cp. 8:11). The Yahwistic naming (Ishmerai — 'YHWH keeps') punctuates the Benjaminite list, a small witness that even after the tribe's near-loss in Judg 20, covenant identity was carried forward through its families.

i-chronicles|8|20.text: 8:20 Elienai, and Zilthai, and Eliel: Three sons of Shimhi (8:21). Like the Yahwistic names in 8:18, these *El*-compounded names (Elienai — 'God is my eyes'; Eliel — 'God is my God') confess theological identity at the level of household naming.

i-chronicles|8|21.text: 8:21 Adaiah, and Beraiah, and Shimrath, the sons of Shimhi: The closing trio of Shimhi's house. *Beraiah* ('YHWH has created') reinforces the line's covenant character. Shimhi himself bears the same name as the Saulite Shimei who would curse David (2 Sam 16:5-13), a common name across the tribe.

i-chronicles|8|23.text: 8:23 Abdon, and Zichri, and Hanan: Three of the eight sons of Shashak (continuing 8:14-25). Hanan ('he is gracious') was also borne by the prophet Jehu's father (1 Kgs 16:1) — common names of grace recur throughout Benjamin and Israel.

i-chronicles|8|24.text: 8:24 Hananiah, and Elam, and Antothijah: Three more of Shashak's sons. *Antothijah* preserves the place-name Anathoth — the priestly city later associated with Jeremiah (Jer 1:1). Personal names and place-names freely cross-pollinate in tribal memory.

i-chronicles|8|25.text: 8:25 Iphedeiah, and Penuel, the sons of Shashak: The closing pair of Shashak's eight sons. *Penuel* ('face of God') echoes Jacob's wrestling-place (Gen 32:30). The Benjaminite genealogy embeds Pentateuchal memory in its families' very names.

i-chronicles|8|27.text: 8:27 Jaresiah, and Eliah, and Zichri, the sons of Jeroham: The last triple within this Benjaminite section before the chapter shifts to Saul's line (8:29-40). The Chronicler has built up Benjamin's full breadth to set Saul's house within a populous, well-documented tribe.

i-chronicles|9|33.text: 9:33 These are the singers, chief of the fathers of the Levites: A summary verse for the Levitical musicians whose lineages occupied chs 6 and 9. *Patarim* — free, released from other duties — marks the singers' full-time consecration to the music of the house. Worship was not part-time among the Levites of David and Solomon.

i-chronicles|13|13.text: 13:13 David brought not the ark home to himself: After Uzzah's death (13:9-10), David halts the procession in fear. The ark's three-month stay at Obed-edom's house (13:14) becomes a teaching interval — the lesson of holiness (cp. Lev 10:1-3) learned before resumption (chs 15–16). Reverence precedes celebration.

i-chronicles|15|28.text: 15:28 All Israel brought up the ark of the covenant with shouting: The successful procession, carried this time by Levites on their shoulders (15:15) as the law required (Exod 25:14). The communal sound — *teruah*, cornet, trumpets, cymbals, psalteries, harps — gathers every register of voice and instrument; worship had finally learned its proper shape.

i-chronicles|16|43.text: 16:43 The people departed every man to his house: After the day of dedication (16:1-42), Israel disperses to ordinary life while the appointed Levites remain at their stations (16:37-42). David himself returns *lebarek et-beito* — to bless his own house, the ordinary household worship that mirrors the great festival.

i-chronicles|17|17.text: 17:17 This was a small thing in thine eyes, O God: David marvels that God has not only granted the present favor of dynasty but spoken of the family's distant future. The phrase *lemerakhok* (for a great while to come) opens onto a horizon beyond David's vision — ultimately fulfilled in the Messiah (Luke 1:32-33).

i-chronicles|17|18.text: 17:18 What can David speak more to thee for the honour of thy servant?: The king's prayer reaches the limits of speech. *Lekavod* (for the honor) signals that God's gift exceeds any return David can offer — exposing the asymmetry of grace and gratitude that runs through the whole prayer.

i-chronicles|17|19.text: 17:19 For thy servant's sake, and according to thine own heart: David grounds the divine kindness not in his merit but in God's character — *kelibekha* (according to thine own heart). The promise to David's house springs from the same source as the call to Abraham: God's freely chosen love (cp. Deut 7:7-8; Eph 1:5).

i-chronicles|17|20.text: 17:20 There is none like thee, neither is there any God beside thee: David's doxology echoes the Shema (Deut 6:4) and Hannah's prayer (1 Sam 2:2). The recital of God's incomparability sets the dynastic promise within the larger story of redemption — a covenant kept by the one God of all the earth.

i-chronicles|17|21.text: 17:21 What one nation in the earth is like thy people Israel: The promise to David is rooted in the prior covenant with the people. *Ge'ulah* — redemption from Egypt — established Israel as God's own, and the Davidic gift extends that founding act forward (cp. 2 Sam 7:23; Titus 2:14).

i-chronicles|17|22.text: 17:22 Thy people Israel didst thou make thine own people for ever: David seals the previous verse with the formula of covenant possession. The Lord's *am* (people) and Israel's *Elohim* (God) form the irreducible covenant pair (cp. Exod 6:7; Jer 31:33; Rev 21:3) that ultimately reaches its fulfillment in the new covenant.

i-chronicles|17|23.text: 17:23 Let the thing that thou hast spoken concerning thy servant be established: David's prayer turns from praise to petition — that God would do as he has promised. *Yeaman* (let it be established) borrows the language of treaty-sealing. David asks for nothing the Lord has not already pledged.

i-chronicles|17|24.text: 17:24 Let it even be established, that thy name may be magnified for ever: The motive of David's petition is the glory of God's name, not personal grandeur. The phrase *yigdal shimkha* shapes a model of kingly prayer — interest tied to God's reputation more than dynastic perpetuity (cp. John 12:28; 17:1).

i-chronicles|17|26.text: 17:26 Now, Lord, thou art God, and hast promised this goodness: The prayer's closing affirmation. David names the promise simply *hatovah* — the good thing — and rests his hope on God's own self-binding word. The dynasty would survive coups, exile, and silence on the same foundation (cp. 2 Sam 7:28; Heb 6:17-18).

i-chronicles|19|14.text: 19:14 Joab and the people that were with him drew nigh before the Syrians: Joab's tactical split (19:10-11) succeeds — the Syrian wing collapses first, and the Ammonite force follows (19:15). The Chronicler preserves the military detail to display the providence underneath Israel's preserving victories during David's reign (cp. 2 Sam 10:13-14).

i-chronicles|19|15.text: 19:15 The children of Ammon saw that the Syrians were fled: A cascading defeat — Ammon retreats once the Syrian mercenaries fail. Joab's brother Abishai drives them into the city while Joab returns to Jerusalem, leaving the broader Syrian campaign for David's own command (19:17-19; cp. 2 Sam 10:14).

i-chronicles|20|7.text: 20:7 Jonathan the son of Shimea David's brother slew him: One of the four giants of Gath (20:4-8) falls to David's nephew. The Chronicler abbreviates the parallel in 2 Sam 21:21, where the same Jonathan appears. The line of David proves capable of producing not only the king-giant-slayer but a household of giant-slayers.

i-chronicles|21|8.text: 21:8 David said unto God, I have sinned greatly: David's confession follows immediately on the realization of his census-sin (21:6-7). The triple admission — sinned, iniquity, foolish — borrows penitential vocabulary from Ps 32 and 51. Real confession names the act for what it is and pleads for divine erasure (cp. Prov 28:13; 1 John 1:9).

i-chronicles|21|10.text: 21:10 I offer thee three things: choose thee one of them: The prophet Gad delivers the unusual oracle of optioned discipline. The three — famine, defeat, plague — match the covenant curses of Lev 26 and Deut 28. David is given the dignity of selecting his discipline, though all three remain within the Lord's hand (21:13).

i-chronicles|21|19.text: 21:19 David went up at the saying of Gad: David obeys the prophet's instruction to build an altar at Ornan's threshing-floor (21:18). The obedience is immediate and unquestioning — a contrast to the autonomy of the census that began the chapter. Restored kings move at prophetic word (cp. 1 Sam 15:22).

i-chronicles|21|21.text: 21:21 As David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David: The Jebusite owner of the threshing-floor greets the king with deep obeisance. The encounter mixes royal authority with priestly humility — David comes not to seize but to purchase, modeling the rightful transaction by which the future temple site enters Israelite possession.

i-chronicles|21|22.text: 21:22 Grant me the place of this threshingfloor: David refuses the gift of the land (21:23-24) and insists on full payment. Worship that costs nothing is unworthy of the Lord — a theological principle the Chronicler underscores as the site of Solomon's temple is being acquired (cp. 2 Sam 24:24; Rom 12:1).

i-chronicles|22|19.text: 22:19 Set your heart and your soul to seek the Lord your God: David's farewell charge to the assembled leaders frames temple-building as an act of seeking — not architecture alone but heart-orientation. The doubled *levavkhem unafshekhem* echoes the Shema (Deut 6:5), making the temple project an extension of love for the Lord.

i-chronicles|25|13.text: 25:13 The sixth to Bukkiah, he, his sons, and his brethren, were twelve: The casting of lots for the twenty-four musical courses (25:9-31) gives every family equal share. Each course numbered twelve men; the symmetry suggests order, fairness, and a deliberate yearlong rotation matching the festival calendar.

i-chronicles|25|15.text: 25:15 The eighth to Jeshaiah: One of the twenty-four divisions established by lot. The Hebrew *goral* (lot) names a method that bypassed human preference and committed assignment to God (cp. Prov 16:33). Even worship's rota was placed under divine choice.

i-chronicles|25|16.text: 25:16 The ninth to Mattaniah: The list moves through Heman's, Asaph's, and Jeduthun's sons in sequence, the casting following the order of the lots' draw. The careful numbering — 1st, 2nd, 3rd, on through 24th — is the same pattern Luke recalls in the priestly courses (Luke 1:5, 8-9).

i-chronicles|25|17.text: 25:17 The tenth to Shimei: The lot-system established a rotating schedule that allowed every Levitical singer to share leadership across the year. No one family monopolized the music; equity in worship was structurally ensured.

i-chronicles|25|18.text: 25:18 The eleventh to Azareel: The continuing list. Azareel means 'God has helped' — a fitting name for one set apart to lead Israel's praise. The Chronicler preserves each singer's name because each was personally consecrated, not interchangeable.

i-chronicles|25|19.text: 25:19 The twelfth to Hashabiah: Half the divisions are now named. The careful tally — twelve down, twelve to go — patterns the temple's worship after twelve tribes, twelve months, and the broader symbolism of completeness (cp. Rev 21:12-14).

i-chronicles|25|20.text: 25:20 The thirteenth to Shubael: The second half of the list opens. Shubael (var. Shebuel) is named earlier as a son of Heman (25:4); his name means 'return to God' and fits the singers' calling to lead the people back into the Lord's presence.

i-chronicles|25|21.text: 25:21 The fourteenth to Mattithiah: Another of Jeduthun's sons (25:3). *Mattithiah* — 'gift of YHWH' — captures the singers' self-understanding: their voice was itself given to them, to be offered back in worship.

i-chronicles|25|22.text: 25:22 The fifteenth to Jeremoth: A son of Heman (25:4). The continuing roll testifies that worship in David's organized temple was not the work of a few stars but of two hundred eighty-eight trained singers (25:7) drawn from many households of Levi.

i-chronicles|25|23.text: 25:23 The sixteenth to Hananiah: The name means 'YHWH has been gracious' and is borne also by one of Daniel's three companions (Dan 1:6). Yahwistic names dominate the list, naming each singer's family theology at the level of personal identity.

i-chronicles|25|24.text: 25:24 The seventeenth to Joshbekashah: Heman's eleventh son (25:4). The unusual name belongs to a string of names David's spirit-led prayer-songs gave to Heman's sons (25:4-5), making the very list of names a hidden hymn of praise.

i-chronicles|25|25.text: 25:25 The eighteenth to Hanani: Heman's twelfth son (25:4). The full set of Heman's fourteen sons mirrors the broader pattern: each one personally named and assigned a course, no service treated as interchangeable.

i-chronicles|25|26.text: 25:26 The nineteenth to Mallothi: The list continues through Heman's house. The Chronicler's care to name every singer matches Paul's later insistence on the irreplaceable particularity of every member of the body (1 Cor 12:14-27).

i-chronicles|25|27.text: 25:27 The twentieth to Eliathah: Heman's son whose name means 'my God has come.' The hymnic resonance of the names continues — every name announced before the people becomes a brief confession in itself.

i-chronicles|25|28.text: 25:28 The one and twentieth to Hothir: Three lots remain. The numeric progression — 21st, 22nd, 23rd, 24th — has reached the point that ancient hearers would have begun to anticipate, knowing twenty-four courses must be filled (cp. 24:7-18 for the priestly courses).

i-chronicles|25|29.text: 25:29 The two and twentieth to Giddalti: 'I have magnified' (the Lord) — Heman's son whose name carries praise into the very enumeration. The list of names doubles as a chain of doxology.

i-chronicles|25|30.text: 25:30 The three and twentieth to Mahazioth: The penultimate lot. Mahazioth means 'visions' — a fitting name for the line of Heman, the king's *roeh* (seer; 25:5). The musical and prophetic gifts overlapped in this family's calling.

i-chronicles|26|3.text: 26:3 Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Elioenai the seventh: Three of the seven sons of Meshelemiah, doorkeeper of the tabernacle (26:1-2). The Korahite line — once cursed in Numbers 16 — now stewards the gates. Restoration of an offending family to honored service is a recurring Chronicles theme (cp. 6:37).

i-chronicles|26|32.text: 26:32 His brethren, men of valour, were two thousand and seven hundred chief fathers: David's east-Jordan administrative network — 2,700 Hebronite leaders set over Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh for both religious and royal matters. The dual jurisdiction (matters of God and king's affairs) shows the integrated theocratic order under David.

i-chronicles|27|19.text: 27:19 Of Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah: of Naphtali, Jerimoth the son of Azriel: Two tribal princes appointed by David. The roster of twelve tribal rulers (27:16-22) shows that Israel's federation was administered tribe by tribe even under monarchy — David's kingdom honored the old tribal structure rather than dissolving it.

i-chronicles|27|20.text: 27:20 Of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Azaziah: of the half tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah: Ephraim is given its own prince distinct from Manasseh's, and the half-tribe of Manasseh west of Jordan its own. The careful subdivision honors Joshua's allotments (Josh 17) and respects the tribal complexity Israel actually carried.

i-chronicles|27|21.text: 27:21 Of the half tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo: of Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner: The eastern half-tribe of Manasseh receives its own prince. Jaasiel's father Abner connects this Benjaminite ruler to the great captain of Saul (1 Sam 14:50) — David integrated families from his predecessor's line.

i-chronicles|27|22.text: 27:22 Of Dan, Azareel the son of Jeroham. These were the princes of the tribes of Israel: The roll closes. The Chronicler notes the omission of Asher and Gad (the count totals only ten of the twelve named tribes), perhaps because of incomplete records or because Levi and one other were excluded from civil administration.

i-kings|6|35.text: 6:35 He carved thereon cherubims and palm trees and open flowers: The doors to the inner sanctuary repeat the motifs of the walls (6:29) — angelic guardians, fruitful palms, and flowering openness. The same triad reappears in Ezekiel's visionary temple (Ezek 41:18) and the new Jerusalem's tree of life (Rev 22:2), figuring restored Eden.

i-kings|21|24.text: 21:24 Him that dieth of Ahab in the city the dogs shall eat: Elijah's oracle pronounces the curse-formula already spoken against the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha (cp. 1 Kgs 14:11; 16:4). Dogs and birds devouring corpses denied honored burial — among the gravest curses in the ancient Near East (cp. Jer 7:33; 16:4).

i-kings|22|45.text: 22:45 Are they not written in the book of the chronicles: The summary-formula closes Jehoshaphat's reign, pointing readers to a fuller royal archive now lost. The repeated formula across Kings (cp. 14:19, 29; 15:7, 23) suggests the book of Kings is itself a theological selection from a larger official record.

i-samuel|18|28.text: 18:28 Saul saw and knew that the Lord was with David: The narrator names what Saul had been resisting since 18:12. Doubled knowledge — the Lord with David, Michal loving David — completes the king's isolation.
