From this verse forward Saul's fear and David's favor mirror each other in inverse proportion (cp. 18:29; 1 Sam 16:14).

ii-chronicles|1|11.text: 1:11 Because this was in thine heart: God commends Solomon's request — not riches or vengeance but wisdom to govern. The verse names the *yetzer* (inclination) of Solomon's heart at the start of his reign. The same heart will later turn elsewhere (1 Kgs 11:4), making this commendation also a tragic measuring-stick.

ii-chronicles|1|12.text: 1:12 Wisdom and knowledge is granted unto thee; and I will give thee riches, and wealth, and honour: The Lord answers Solomon with the requested gift plus the unasked. The pattern of generous addition (cp. Matt 6:33) frames Solomon's reign — he received what he sought and more, the wisdom proving his enduring legacy when riches faded.

ii-chronicles|3|7.text: 3:7 He overlaid also the house, the beams, the posts, and the walls thereof, and the doors thereof, with gold: The interior of Solomon's temple was gilded throughout. The gold did not merely decorate — it reflected light from the lamps in a continuous brilliance, signaling that the house was set apart for the Lord's presence (cp. Hag 2:7-9).

ii-chronicles|4|10.text: 4:10 He set the sea on the right side of the east end: The molten sea, ten cubits across (4:2), is positioned south-east of the temple entrance for the priests' ablutions. The sea's vast capacity — three thousand baths (4:5) — provided water for the daily cleansings that no service could omit (cp. Exod 30:18-21).

ii-chronicles|4|20.text: 4:20 The candlesticks with their lamps, that they should burn after the manner before the oracle: Ten gold lampstands (4:7) replace the single tabernacle menorah, multiplying the perpetual light before the inner sanctuary. The lamps burned continually (cp. Lev 24:2; Exod 27:20-21), figuring the constant divine illumination of Israel's worship.

ii-chronicles|5|6.text: 5:6 King Solomon, and all the congregation of Israel: The ark's procession to the temple is a national event. Sacrifices innumerable accompany the move — the same lavish offering that marked David's earlier procession (1 Chr 15:26; 16:1). Worship at this scale signaled that Israel had reached the rest the Lord had promised (cp. 1 Kgs 5:4; Heb 4:8-9).

ii-chronicles|6|3.text: 6:3 The king turned his face, and blessed the whole congregation: Solomon takes the priestly posture of blessing the people (cp. Num 6:23-27; 1 Kgs 8:14). The king's role in the dedication liturgy mixes royal and priestly functions, foreshadowing the messianic priest-king of Ps 110:4 and Heb 7:1-3.

ii-chronicles|6|7.text: 6:7 It was in the heart of David my father to build an house: Solomon recalls his father's intention before recounting the divine prohibition (6:8). The temple stands as a fulfilled inheritance — David desired, God deferred to Solomon, and the son completes what the father envisioned (cp. 1 Chr 22:7-10).

ii-chronicles|6|8.text: 6:8 The Lord said to David my father, Forasmuch as it was in thine heart: God commends the desire even while withholding the doing. The principle resounds: intention pleases God where execution is providentially deferred (cp. 2 Cor 8:12; Heb 11:39-40). The temple was not David's failure but David's bequest.

ii-chronicles|6|9.text: 6:9 Notwithstanding thou shalt not build the house: The prohibition redirects the labor to David's son. The reason (David's wars; 1 Chr 22:8) is theological as well as practical — the house of peace would not arise from hands that had shed much blood. Solomon's name *shalom* foreshadows the role only he could fill.

ii-chronicles|6|15.text: 6:15 Thou which hast kept with thy servant David that which thou hast promised: Solomon's prayer rests on covenant faithfulness already shown. God has *shamarta* — kept — his earlier word; the petition for further keeping is grounded in the proven record (cp. 1 Chr 17:23-27). Memory of past mercy fuels present hope.

ii-chronicles|6|16.text: 6:16 There shall not fail thee a man in my sight to sit upon the throne of Israel: Solomon recites the dynastic promise of 1 Chr 17:12-14 with the conditional clause — *if* the sons walk in the law. The promise is sure; the manner of its fulfillment depends on obedience. Christ ultimately satisfies both promise and condition (Heb 1:8-9).

ii-chronicles|6|17.text: 6:17 Let thy word be verified, which thou hast spoken: Solomon asks for divine ratification (*ye'amen*) of the very word the Lord himself gave. The prayer is recursive: God is asked to do what he has promised — the highest form of trust, leaning on his own faithfulness alone.

ii-chronicles|6|19.text: 6:19 Have respect therefore to the prayer of thy servant: The phrase *uphanita el-tefillat* (turn unto the prayer) repeats throughout the temple-dedication prayer (cp. 6:20, 21, 23). The temple is established as the place toward which Israel's prayer is to be directed — and from which God's answer comes (cp. 6:21; Dan 6:10).

ii-chronicles|6|20.text: 6:20 That thine eyes may be open upon this house day and night: Solomon's petition that the temple be the focus of continuous divine attention. The Lord himself promises this response in 7:15-16. The temple becomes the meeting-place of heaven's gaze and earth's voice — a typological forerunner of the incarnate Lord (John 1:14).

ii-chronicles|6|40.text: 6:40 Now, my God, let thine eyes be open, and thine ears be attent: Solomon's closing summary repeats the opening petition (6:20). The prayer is bracketed by the same plea — eyes seeing, ears attending — that the house function as designed: a place where the worshiper's voice reaches a hearing God (cp. 1 Pet 3:12).

ii-chronicles|7|11.text: 7:11 Solomon finished the house of the Lord, and the king's house: The summary couples temple and palace as a single twenty-year project (1 Kgs 9:10). The phrase *kol haba al-leb Shelomoh* — all that came into Solomon's heart — signals successful execution of vision, but also foreshadows the divided heart that will later betray him (1 Kgs 11:1-4).

ii-chronicles|7|16.text: 7:16 I have chosen and sanctified this house, that my name may be there for ever: God's response to Solomon's prayer affirms the permanence of his presence at the temple — *le'olam*, for ever. The promise survives the temple's destruction; even after exile the place itself remains chosen, anchoring the post-exilic return (Ezra 1:3).

ii-chronicles|8|8.text: 8:8 But of their children, who were left after them in the land: Solomon's labor force drew on the remaining Canaanite populations, a continuation of Israel's incomplete conquest (Josh 17:13; Judg 1:28-35). The Chronicler notes that native Israelites were not enslaved (8:9), preserving covenant freedom while organizing the realm.

ii-chronicles|8|16.text: 8:16 All the work of Solomon was prepared unto the day of the foundation of the house of the Lord: The summary statement that closes the temple-construction narrative. The phrase *neshlemah* (perfected) plays on Solomon's name — the man of peace completed the work of peace, mirroring the messianic peace yet to come (Eph 2:14-22).

ii-chronicles|9|5.text: 9:5 It was a true report which I heard in mine own land: The queen of Sheba's testimony confirms what reached her by hearsay. *Ne'eman hadavar* — the word was sure — anticipates a deeper pattern: God's report of his wisdom reaches the nations, and the seeker who travels to verify it always finds more than the rumor promised (cp. Matt 12:42).

ii-chronicles|9|6.text: 9:6 The one half of the greatness of thy wisdom was not told me: Sheba's confession that report could not capture reality. *Lo huggad-li* — it was not told me — names the limit of secondhand knowledge. The same surplus marks every encounter with the wisdom that comes from God; sight outruns rumor (cp. John 1:18; 1 Cor 2:9).

ii-chronicles|9|7.text: 9:7 Happy are thy men, and happy are these thy servants: The queen blesses Solomon's household for proximity to wisdom. The doubled *ashre* (happy, blessed) frames daily presence in Solomon's court as a privileged state — a foretaste of the disciples' privilege to dwell with one greater than Solomon (Matt 12:42; Luke 10:23-24).

ii-chronicles|9|8.text: 9:8 Blessed be the Lord thy God, which delighted in thee to set thee on his throne: The queen redirects praise from king to King-maker. *Kisse YHWH* — the Lord's throne — names the Davidic seat as God's own; the human king is steward, not owner (cp. 1 Chr 29:23). The foreign queen articulates a theology Israel itself sometimes forgot.

ii-chronicles|9|10.text: 9:10 The servants of Huram, and the servants of Solomon, which brought gold from Ophir: The maritime partnership with Tyre (cp. 2 Chr 8:18) brought rare goods from Ophir — a location debated by historians, possibly in southern Arabia or East Africa. Algum (almug) wood, scarce and aromatic, suited the temple's adornment.

ii-chronicles|9|11.text: 9:11 The king made of the algum trees terraces to the house of the Lord: Solomon used the imported wood for temple stairs and royal harps — sacred craft and royal music drawing on the same rare material. The verse closes by stressing the unprecedented quality of the supply; covenant blessing tied to obedience produced visible abundance.

ii-chronicles|9|20.text: 9:20 All the drinking vessels of king Solomon were of gold: The royal table itself displayed the era's abundance. Silver was *lo nehshav* — not reckoned of value — in Solomon's day. The detail signals fulfillment of the blessing of 1:12, but also sets up the eventual loss recorded as the kingdom divides (cp. 1 Kgs 14:25-26).

ii-chronicles|9|23.text: 9:23 All the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon, to hear his wisdom: The breadth of Solomon's renown — kings of the earth come to him. The pattern foreshadows the eschatological pilgrimage of the nations to Zion (Isa 2:2-3; Mic 4:1-2; Matt 2:1-2), the wisdom of Solomon a faint type of the wisdom of Christ.

ii-chronicles|9|24.text: 9:24 They brought every man his present: vessels of silver, and vessels of gold: The recurring tribute fed the kingdom's treasury year by year. *Minhah* — gift or tribute — was the standard token of vassal submission in the ancient Near East. Solomon's empire stood at its peak, surrounded by kings sending annual gifts.

ii-chronicles|9|26.text: 9:26 He reigned over all the kings from the river even unto the land of the Philistines: The Euphrates to Egypt's border — fulfillment of the boundary promise of Gen 15:18. Solomon's reign briefly realized the largest extent of Israel's territory in history, though the dominion was through suzerainty more than direct rule (cp. 1 Kgs 4:21).

ii-chronicles|9|27.text: 9:27 The king made silver in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar trees as the sycomore trees: Hyperbole names a real economic reality — silver so abundant it was unremarked, and cedar (an expensive import) as common as the native sycamore. Material prosperity overflowed the capital under Solomon's wisdom (cp. 1 Kgs 10:27).

ii-chronicles|9|31.text: 9:31 Solomon slept with his fathers, and he was buried in the city of David: The conventional regnal closing. *Shakhav im-avotav* (slept with his fathers) frames death as gathered company rather than annihilation. Solomon's forty-year reign (9:30) ends; Rehoboam inherits a kingdom about to split.

ii-chronicles|10|5.text: 10:5 Come again unto me after three days: Rehoboam asks for time to weigh the people's request for relief from forced labor (10:4). The three-day delay would have allowed humble consultation; instead it became the space in which Rehoboam chose poorly between elder and younger counselors (10:6-11).

ii-chronicles|10|9.text: 10:9 What advice give ye that we may return answer to this people?: Rehoboam puts the same question to his younger counselors that he had put to the older (10:6). The narrative deliberately reveals his uncertainty — wisdom would have weighed both, but the king already had his preference and was looking for confirmation rather than counsel.

ii-chronicles|10|13.text: 10:13 The king answered them roughly; and king Rehoboam forsook the counsel of the old men: *Qashah* — to make hard, harsh — names the king's chosen tone. Forsaking the elders' counsel is the formal pivot of the chapter; from this moment the kingdom is positioned to split. Hardness against the people will cost Rehoboam ten tribes (cp. Prov 15:1).

ii-chronicles|10|14.text: 10:14 My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions: The boasting threat — heavy whips called scorpions, perhaps tipped with metal — escalates Solomon's labor regime rather than easing it. Rehoboam misreads the political moment, supposing strength lies in cruelty; the very next verse records the people's rejection.

ii-chronicles|10|17.text: 10:17 As for the children of Israel that dwelt in the cities of Judah, Rehoboam reigned over them: The first formal mention of the divided kingdom under its new name. *Yisra'el* (Israel) shifts in this verse to the northern tribes only; *Yehudah* (Judah) becomes the residual kingdom of the south. The geographical and theological terms reshape the rest of Israel's story.

ii-chronicles|16|5.text: 16:5 When Baasha heard it, that he left off building of Ramah: Asa's bribe to Ben-hadad of Syria (16:2-4) succeeds militarily — Baasha abandons the fortification of Ramah. But the prophet Hanani's rebuke (16:7-9) names the trust-failure: Asa relied on Syria, not the Lord, and the victory is reckoned a deeper loss.

ii-chronicles|16|13.text: 16:13 Asa slept with his fathers, and died in the one and fortieth year of his reign: Asa's long reign closes after the prophetic confrontation, the disease in his feet (16:12), and the recourse to physicians instead of the Lord. The Chronicler softens the regnal close with funeral honors (16:14) while preserving the theological warning.

ii-chronicles|18|8.text: 18:8 The king of Israel called for one of his officers, and said, Fetch quickly Micaiah: Ahab summons the prophet whose oracle he does not want (18:7). The naming of the messenger — and the haste — set up the tension. Truth-tellers are recalled only when court-prophets have already filled the room with comforting lies.

ii-chronicles|18|10.text: 18:10 Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah had made him horns of iron: A prophetic act-symbol — iron horns to figure Israel pushing Syria back. The visual aid amplifies a false oracle (cp. Jer 23:30-32). Even effective theater cannot give the spirit of true prophecy; the spectacle's confidence outran its truth.

ii-chronicles|18|11.text: 18:11 All the prophets prophesied so: The court chorus reinforces Zedekiah's word (18:10). Numbers do not establish truth — four hundred against one (18:7) was the wrong arithmetic. The pattern recurs in Israel: the prophet of God often stood alone (cp. 1 Kgs 18:22; Jer 26:7-19).

ii-chronicles|18|12.text: 18:12 The messenger spake to him, saying, Behold, the words of the prophets declare good: The messenger urges Micaiah toward conformity with the court consensus. The pressure is sociological, not theological — *davar tov* (a good word) is what the king wants to hear. The pressure to flatter is one of prophecy's oldest temptations (cp. 2 Tim 4:3).

ii-chronicles|18|13.text: 18:13 As the Lord liveth, even what my God saith, that will I speak: Micaiah's standing answer to the messenger. *Hai-YHWH* — the oath formula — binds his speech to God's word alone. The verse is the prophetic charter: a true messenger has surrendered the right to choose his content (cp. Num 22:18; Jer 23:28).

ii-chronicles|18|14.text: 18:14 Go ye up, and prosper: Micaiah at first parrots the false oracle ironically. The king himself recognizes the mockery and adjures him to speak truth (18:15) — a tacit admission that Ahab knew all along he was being told what he wanted to hear, and only now demanded the real word.

ii-chronicles|18|16.text: 18:16 I did see all Israel scattered upon the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd: Micaiah's true vision — Israel without a king after the battle. The image of shepherdless sheep recurs (cp. Num 27:17; Ezek 34:5; Matt 9:36), naming a community without provision and protection. The oracle predicts Ahab's death (18:34).

ii-chronicles|18|17.text: 18:17 Did I not tell thee that he would not prophesy good unto me, but evil?: Ahab confirms to Jehoshaphat that he had expected the unwelcome word. The verse exposes the king's double mind — he had hoped to hear comfort, while knowing comfort was unwarranted. The willful blindness will not save him from the truth's outcome.

ii-chronicles|18|23.text: 18:23 Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near, and smote Micaiah upon the cheek: The false prophet strikes the true. Physical violence against the truth-teller foreshadows the suffering pattern of all faithful prophecy — culminating in the Lord himself struck before the Sanhedrin (Mic 5:1; John 18:22; Acts 23:2).

ii-chronicles|18|24.text: 18:24 Behold, thou shalt see on that day when thou shalt go into an inner chamber to hide thyself: Micaiah's reply — the day will come when Zedekiah hides for fear. Vindication awaits the prophet of the Lord; the false prophet who flourishes in public will end in private terror (cp. Jer 28:15-17).

ii-chronicles|18|27.text: 18:27 If thou certainly return in peace, then hath not the Lord spoken by me: Micaiah stakes his prophetic legitimacy on the outcome — the Deuteronomic test of prophecy (Deut 18:22). Ahab does not return; the test resolves in Micaiah's favor (18:33-34), though the king is too dead to recognize the verdict.

ii-chronicles|23|10.text: 23:10 He set all the people, every man having his weapon in his hand: Jehoiada's coronation of the boy-king Joash is protected by armed Levites stationed around the temple. The unusual arming of the worshipers reflects the fragility of restoration — the rightful Davidic line had to be defended even within the house of the Lord (cp. 23:6-9).

ii-chronicles|23|20.text: 23:20 He took the captains of hundreds, and the nobles: The procession from temple to palace formally installs Joash. The order — through the high gate into the king's house — re-establishes the divinely ordained pattern: priesthood escorts the Davidic king from his consecration to his throne (cp. 1 Kgs 1:38-40).

ii-chronicles|24|2.text: 24:2 Joash did that which was right in the sight of the Lord all the days of Jehoiada the priest: The qualifier *kol-yemei Yehoyada* (all the days of Jehoiada) foreshadows the king's later collapse after the priest's death (24:17-22). Joash's faithfulness was borrowed, not owned — a sober warning about religion shaped by another's piety alone.

ii-chronicles|25|19.text: 25:19 Thou sayest, Lo, thou hast smitten the Edomites: King Joash of Israel's letter to Amaziah of Judah mixes mockery and warning. The Edomite victory (25:5-13) had inflated Amaziah's pride; Joash names it. Both kings are flawed, but Joash's caution prevails — pride blinds Amaziah to the disproportion of his coming defeat (cp. Prov 16:18).

ii-chronicles|25|22.text: 25:22 Judah was put to the worse before Israel: The battle at Beth-shemesh fulfills Joash's warning. Amaziah's army is routed, the king himself captured (25:23), and Jerusalem's wall partly broken down (25:24). Royal pride brought royal humiliation — a pattern Chronicles draws repeatedly to warn future kings.

ii-chronicles|25|25.text: 25:25 Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah lived after the death of Joash king of Israel fifteen years: A regnal note preserving Amaziah's outliving of his Israelite rival. The fifteen-year remainder, however, ends in conspiracy and death (25:27-28) — the same pattern of unrestored relationship with the Lord that Chronicles names again and again.

ii-chronicles|25|28.text: 25:28 They brought him upon horses, and buried him with his fathers: The dignified return of Amaziah's corpse to Jerusalem. The Chronicler permits the burial honors (cp. 1 Kgs 14:13) while preserving the assassination narrative (25:27). Closure of the regnal account does not erase the verdict on the reign.

ii-chronicles|26|4.text: 26:4 He did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his father Amaziah did: The double-edged formula. Amaziah did right but not with a perfect heart (25:2); Uzziah inherits the same partial obedience. The Chronicler's reign-evaluations measure not only outward conformity but the heart's whole orientation.

ii-chronicles|27|8.text: 27:8 He was five and twenty years old when he began to reign, and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem: A standard regnal summary for Jotham. The age and tenure pair to give a king's typological measure — the same data Kings supplies (cp. 2 Kgs 15:33), preserved by the Chronicler within his theological frame.

ii-chronicles|27|9.text: 27:9 Jotham slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David: Jotham's faithful reign closes peacefully — *vayyishkav* (he slept) with the patriarchal-kingly burial in the city of David. The Chronicler's verdict was strong (27:6); Ahaz inherits the throne but not the obedience.

ii-chronicles|28|2.text: 28:2 He walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, and made also molten images for Baalim: Ahaz's idolatry is identified by its northern model — the kings of Israel rather than the kings of David. The Chronicler names Baal-worship by Ahaz the southern king, a syncretism that would invite the prophetic verdicts of Isaiah and Micah (cp. Isa 7:1-14; Mic 1:5).

ii-chronicles|29|35.text: 29:35 The burnt offerings were in abundance, with the fat of the peace offerings, and the drink offerings: Hezekiah's reformation peaks in a flood of restored offerings. The Chronicler closes the chapter with *vattikkon avodat beit-YHWH* — the service of the Lord's house was established. Restoration is measured by the resumption of right worship.

ii-chronicles|33|8.text: 33:8 Neither will I any more remove the foot of Israel from out of the land: The Lord's promise to Solomon (cp. 2 Chr 7:18) is recalled even in the Manasseh narrative — the conditional preservation that Manasseh's idolatry endangers. The promise's *if* (Solomon obeys the law) becomes Manasseh's *but* (Manasseh did not), and exile draws near.

ii-chronicles|33|9.text: 33:9 Manasseh made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to err, and to do worse than the heathen: The Chronicler's harshest verdict on any Judahite king. Manasseh exceeded even the dispossessed Canaanites in evil. The judgment sets the stage for the prophet Jeremiah's later naming of Manasseh as the precipitating cause of exile (Jer 15:4; 2 Kgs 21:11-15).

ii-chronicles|34|20.text: 34:20 The king commanded Hilkiah, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan: Josiah dispatches a delegation of five men — three Levitical/scribal officials, a royal servant, and the high priest — to inquire of the Lord. The careful staffing of the embassy signals the seriousness with which Josiah received the rediscovered law (cp. 2 Kgs 22:12-14).

ii-chronicles|34|21.text: 34:21 Great is the wrath of the Lord that is poured out upon us: Josiah's reading of the law recognizes that judgment had already accumulated. *Khamah gedolah* — great fury — was named in Deut 29:28 as the curse for covenant-breaking. Josiah sees that the curses had begun and seeks oracle to know what remains.

ii-chronicles|34|23.text: 34:23 Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Tell ye the man that sent you: Huldah the prophetess opens her oracle with the standard messenger formula. The phrase *ha'ish asher shelach etkhem* — the man that sent you — preserves a deliberate distance: the queen of prophets does not honor the king's title, only the message that must reach him.

ii-chronicles|34|25.text: 34:25 Because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods: Huldah's oracle names the cause of coming judgment in unambiguous terms. The verbs *azevuni* (forsaken me) and *vayyaqtiru* (burned incense) recall the covenant indictment of the prophets (cp. Jer 1:16). The wrath *titaq* — poured out — fulfills Deut 29:23.

ii-chronicles|34|26.text: 34:26 As for the king of Judah, who sent you to enquire of the Lord: Huldah pivots from the general indictment to a personal word for Josiah. The Lord noticed his humble inquiry (34:27) and tempers the verdict — judgment will come, but not in Josiah's days. Personal repentance buys reprieve, though not escape, from corporate consequence.

ii-chronicles|35|26.text: 35:26 The rest of the acts of Josiah, and his goodness, according to that which was written in the law of the Lord: The closing formula for Josiah measures him by the very book his reign rediscovered. *Wahasadav* — his acts of covenant-faithfulness — are evaluated by the standard he himself reintroduced. No higher epitaph could be written.

ii-chronicles|36|7.text: 36:7 Nebuchadnezzar also carried of the vessels of the house of the Lord to Babylon: The first wave of temple vessels travels to Babylon under Jehoiakim (605 BC). The image of *kelei beit-YHWH* dispersed among foreign temples becomes a recurring grief (cp. Dan 1:2; 5:2-3; Ezra 1:7-11). The return of these vessels will mark restoration.

ii-chronicles|36|8.text: 36:8 The rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and his abominations: The Chronicler abbreviates Jehoiakim's eleven-year reign with the brief *vetoavotav* — and his abominations — leaving the catalogue to Jeremiah and 2 Kings. *Mah-shenimtsa alav* (what was found in him) hints at unspecified darkness; Jehoiachin succeeds his father into a kingdom three months from exile.

ii-kings|2|25.text: 2:25 He went from thence to mount Carmel, and from thence he returned to Samaria: Elisha's circuit after the Bethel encounter (2:23-24) — Carmel as Elijah's old prophetic stronghold (1 Kgs 18:19-20), Samaria as the capital where his ministry will engage kings. The verse maps the geographical scope of Elisha's office, succeeding Elijah's.

ii-kings|10|35.text: 10:35 Jehu slept with his fathers: and they buried him in Samaria: Jehu's twenty-eight-year reign closes (10:36). The Chronicler's editor notes the regular honors of burial despite the mixed verdict on Jehu's reign — zealous against Baal but indifferent to the calves of Bethel and Dan (10:29-31).

ii-kings|10|36.text: 10:36 The time that Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria was twenty and eight years: A regnal-tenure summary for the founder of the longest dynasty in the northern kingdom (cp. 15:12 — four generations). The promise honored Jehu's partial obedience; the dynasty's eventual end at Zechariah (15:8-12) honored the limit of that obedience.

ii-kings|15|28.text: 15:28 He did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord: The standard verdict on Pekah of Israel — twenty years (15:27) of unbroken continuity in the sins of Jeroboam. The pattern of relentless northern apostasy moves the kingdom toward Tiglath-pileser's invasion (15:29) and ultimately the fall of Samaria (17:6).

ii-kings|15|31.text: 15:31 The rest of the acts of Pekah are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel: The conventional closing formula for the kings of the north. The cited royal records — the books of the chronicles of Israel and of Judah — are sources distinct from the canonical Chronicles, now lost.

ii-kings|15|38.text: 15:38 Jotham slept with his fathers: A peaceful closure for Jotham's sixteen-year reign in Judah. Faithful, though imperfect (cp. 15:35), Jotham bequeaths the kingdom to Ahaz, under whom Judah's worst idolatry will resume — the dynastic line preserved despite the moral trajectory faltering.

ii-kings|20|14.text: 20:14 Then came Isaiah the prophet unto king Hezekiah: The prophetic visit follows Hezekiah's reception of the Babylonian envoys (20:12-13). Isaiah's question — what said these men? — is the opening of a confrontation that will unmask the king's vanity in showing his treasures (20:15-18). Prophecy interrogates the king's choices.

ii-kings|20|15.text: 20:15 What have they seen in thine house? And Hezekiah answered, All the things: The king's reply is candid but incriminating. *Kol asher beveiti* — all that is in my house — names a comprehensive disclosure to a foreign power. Hezekiah's pride in his treasury (cp. Isa 39:2) foreshadows Babylon's later carrying of the same wealth into captivity.

ii-kings|20|16.text: 20:16 Hear the word of the Lord: Isaiah's prophetic formula opens the rebuke (20:17-18) — the very treasures shown will be carried to Babylon, and Hezekiah's descendants will serve as eunuchs in that king's palace. The oracle fulfills in 2 Kgs 24:13 (Jehoiachin) and Dan 1:3-7 (royal youths in Babylon).

ii-kings|20|21.text: 20:21 Hezekiah slept with his fathers: and Manasseh his son reigned in his stead: Hezekiah's twenty-nine-year reign closes. The succession to Manasseh, who reverses every reform (cp. 21:1-9), is the most painful pivot in the Davidic line — a faithful father followed by the worst of his sons. The contrast underscores covenant's generation-by-generation contingency.

ii-samuel|21|22.text: 21:22 These four were born to the giant in Gath: The closing summary of the four-Philistine-giant accounts (21:15-22). David's mighty men kill the giants of Gath one by one; the king is preserved from death because his servants stand between him and the threat (cp. 21:17). The kingdom's mighties protect the anointed.

ii-samuel|22|28.text: 22:28 The afflicted people thou wilt save: but thine eyes are upon the haughty: A two-line theology of God's preferential look. *Ani* (afflicted) — the same word used in the Beatitudes' Greek echo (Matt 5:3-5; Luke 1:52-53). The Lord's eyes both elevate the lowly and bring down the lofty (Ps 18:27; Jas 4:6).

ii-samuel|22|33.text: 22:33 God is my strength and power: and he maketh my way perfect: The doubled praise — *ma'uzzi* (my strength) and *darki tamim* (perfect path). The verbs cast all the king's success on the Lord. David ends his life (cp. ch. 22 sung in the king's old age) attributing every victory not to military skill but to divine sustenance.

ii-samuel|22|35.text: 22:35 He teacheth my hands to war; so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms: The Lord's instruction reaches even technique — *yedei lammilkhamah* (hands to war). Bronze (not steel; the Hebrew *nehushah* signals the metal) bows were ornamental, marking the verse's hyperbole — the king's strength stretches beyond the natural by divine empowerment (cp. Ps 18:34).

ii-samuel|22|37.text: 22:37 Thou hast enlarged my steps under me; so that my feet did not slip: The wide path under the warrior's feet is God's gift of stability. The image — *tahteni* (under me) — names the supporting ground beneath each step. The same metaphor encourages perseverance in the psalter (Ps 18:36; Prov 4:12).

ii-samuel|22|41.text: 22:41 Thou hast also given me the necks of mine enemies: The bowed neck in ancient warfare signaled subjugation. David ascribes the defeat of opposition not to his sword but to the Lord's giving (*natatah-li*). The same conviction underwrites Paul's later doxology — *not I, but the grace of God* (1 Cor 15:10).

ii-samuel|22|43.text: 22:43 Then did I beat them as small as the dust of the earth: The hyperbole of total triumph — enemies reduced to dust and street-mire. The image, though violent to modern ears, was conventional in royal annals; David's poem nevertheless gives the Lord the agency throughout, refusing self-celebration even in victory.

ii-samuel|22|45.text: 22:45 Strangers shall submit themselves unto me: as soon as they hear, they shall be obedient: The reach of David's reign extends beyond Israel by reputation alone. *Bnei nekhar* (sons of foreign nations) submit by ear, not encounter — a faint type of the Messiah's wider rule, accomplished through proclamation reaching the nations (Rom 10:14-17).

ii-samuel|22|46.text: 22:46 Strangers shall fade away, and they shall be afraid out of their close places: The corollary — those who do not submit fade. *Wechorgu* (will be afraid) names the dread that drives foreign princes from their strongholds at the news of God's anointed. The verses anticipate the global response to Christ's rule (cp. Ps 2:10-12).

ii-samuel|22|48.text: 22:48 It is God that avengeth me, and that bringeth down the people under me: The vengeance belongs to God, not the king (cp. Deut 32:35; Rom 12:19). David positions himself as the vehicle of justice, not its source. The verb *moridem* (bringing down) preserves divine agency at every level of military and political success.

ii-samuel|22|49.text: 22:49 That bringeth me forth from mine enemies: thou also hast lifted me up: The doubled action — out of enemies' hands, up above their rising. The psalm's larger arc moves from sinking-in-distress (22:5-7) to lifted-on-high (22:49), tracing the rescue pattern God works for his anointed. Paul reads it as fulfilled in Christ (Rom 15:9).

joshua|13|33.text: 13:33 Unto the tribe of Levi Moses gave not any inheritance: the Lord God of Israel was their inheritance: The closing note on the eastern tribal allotments. Levi's portion is named in 13:14 and 33; the principle — *YHWH...nahalatam* — sets a theological standard for ministry. The priestly tribe stands among Israel without ownership in it, sustained by the people's tithes (cp. Num 18:20-24; Deut 18:1-2).

judges|11|40.text: 11:40 The daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in a year: The annual lamentation memorializes Jephthah's daughter (11:29-40). The four-day rite — preserved nowhere else in Israel — registers a tragedy the narrative does not approve. Whether the daughter was sacrificed or dedicated to perpetual virginity is debated; either way, Israel remembered.

leviticus|4|9.text: 4:9 The two kidneys, and the fat that is upon them, which is by the flanks: The sacrificial portion offered for the anointed-priest's unintentional sin. The internal fat — *kelayot* (kidneys) and *yotereth* (caul above the liver) — was reserved for the Lord throughout the sacrificial system (cp. Lev 3:4, 10, 15). The most hidden parts were given first.

leviticus|4|10.text: 4:10 As it was taken off from the bullock of the sacrifice of peace offerings: The sin-offering's procedure mirrors the peace-offering's regarding the fat (Lev 3:3-5). The deliberate parallel signals a theological point — confession and communion follow the same liturgical grammar; sin offered up makes way for fellowship at the table (cp. 1 John 1:9-2:1).

leviticus|4|17.text: 4:17 The priest shall dip his finger in some of the blood, and sprinkle it seven times before the Lord: The sevenfold sprinkling before the inner veil is reserved for the most serious cases — the priest's own sin and the congregation's (cp. 4:6). Seven figures completeness; the blood-rite was a full act of expiation, not a partial one.

leviticus|4|18.text: 4:18 He shall put some of the blood upon the horns of the altar which is before the Lord: The horns of the inner altar — the altar of incense, not the bronze altar of burnt offering. The blood's placement on the place where intercession went up to God (cp. Exod 30:1-10) marked the comprehensive reach of the sin offering into the holy place itself.

leviticus|4|19.text: 4:19 He shall take all his fat from him, and burn it upon the altar: All the inner fat — heart, kidneys, liver-coverings — is offered. *Khelev* (fat) is repeatedly named the Lord's portion (cp. Lev 3:16). The fire on the altar consumes what represents inner substance, signifying that sin's expiation reaches into the body's hidden depths.

leviticus|4|21.text: 4:21 He shall carry forth the bullock without the camp, and burn him as he burned the first bullock: it is a sin offering for the congregation: The bullock's burning *outside the camp* sets a pattern that Hebrews will read christologically — *Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate* (Heb 13:11-12). The congregation's sin pushed its offering outside the holy circle.

leviticus|8|24.text: 8:24 Moses put of the blood upon the tip of their right ear, and upon the thumbs of their right hands, and upon the great toes of their right feet: The triple-point anointing of Aaron's sons consecrates ear (to hear God's word), hand (to perform priestly service), and foot (to walk in holy paths). The whole bodily life is set apart at three deliberate points (cp. Lev 14:14, 17 for parallel cleansing of a healed leper).

leviticus|8|25.text: 8:25 He took the fat, and the rump, and all the fat that was upon the inwards: The ram of consecration's inner fats — given wholly to the Lord. The detail repeats Leviticus's central pattern: the priest, like the sin offering, surrenders the hidden inner substance to God. Consecration is from the inside out.

leviticus|14|50.text: 14:50 He shall kill the one of the birds in an earthen vessel over running water: The cleansing of a *zarua* (afflicted) house mirrors the rite for a cleansed leper (14:5). One bird dies; the other will be dipped in the blood and released. The doubled image — death and freedom — figures cleansing as both atonement and liberation (cp. 14:6-7).

leviticus|14|51.text: 14:51 He shall take the cedar wood, and the hyssop, and the scarlet, and the living bird, and dip them in the blood: The same four-element bundle (cedar, hyssop, scarlet, living bird) appears in the leper's cleansing (14:6) and the red-heifer rite (Num 19:6). The recurrence ties the various cleansings into a single sacramental vocabulary of restoration.

leviticus|14|52.text: 14:52 He shall cleanse the house with the blood of the bird, and with the running water, and with the living bird, and with the cedar wood, and with the hyssop, and with the scarlet: The thorough cleansing of the *bayit* (house) returns it to ordinary use. *Khitte'* (he shall purify) is used here for an inanimate dwelling — sacred space-making extended past tabernacle to the home, where holiness could be honored daily.

leviticus|16|34.text: 16:34 An everlasting statute, to make an atonement for the children of Israel for all their sins once a year: The Day of Atonement's annual cycle. *Khuqqat olam* — perpetual statute — names the rhythm of national repentance and renewed standing before God. Hebrews reads the day's limitation (only once a year, with no real removal) as the precondition for Christ's once-for-all atonement (Heb 9:25-26).

luke|3|29.text: 3:29 Which was the son of Jose, which was the son of Eliezer, which was the son of Jorim: Names in Jesus' Lukan genealogy between David and Zerubbabel. Luke's list (3:23-38) traces Jesus through Nathan, son of David, rather than through Solomon (cp. Matt 1:6), preserving a distinct line that grounds the legal succession differently.

luke|3|30.text: 3:30 Which was the son of Simeon, which was the son of Juda, which was the son of Joseph, which was the son of Jonan: Luke's ascending genealogy continues toward the patriarchs. The unfamiliar names — none mentioned elsewhere in Scripture — preserve a record otherwise lost. Their inclusion testifies that Luke worked from a careful source (cp. Luke 1:1-4).

luke|3|33.text: 3:33 Which was the son of Aminadab, which was the son of Aram, which was the son of Esrom, which was the son of Phares, which was the son of Juda: The Lukan line meets the Davidic line at these four shared names (cp. Ruth 4:18-22; Matt 1:3-4). Luke now joins the recognized covenant chain — Jesus' descent from Judah through David is firmly recorded.

luke|3|34.text: 3:34 Which was the son of Jacob, which was the son of Isaac, which was the son of Abraham, which was the son of Thara, which was the son of Nachor: The line traverses the patriarchs and pushes back through Terah to Nahor. Luke's deliberate extension past Abraham to Adam (3:38) frames Jesus as son of the whole human race, not merely of Israel — universalizing his messianic identity (cp. Rom 5:14-19).

luke|9|60.text: 9:60 Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God: Jesus' apparent harshness names a deeper priority — discipleship outranks even the most sacred family duties (cp. Matt 8:22). The *nekrous* (dead) who bury the dead may name those spiritually unalive to the kingdom; the disciple is called to its proclamation without delay.

luke|11|54.text: 11:54 Laying wait for him, and seeking to catch something out of his mouth, that they might accuse him: The scribes and Pharisees move from theological objection to forensic ambush. *Enedreuontes* (laying wait) is hunters' vocabulary. The verse closes the conflict-cycle of Luke 11 and prepares for the broader hostility that culminates at the cross.

luke|18|42.text: 18:42 Receive thy sight: thy faith hath saved thee: Jesus' word to the Jericho beggar (18:35-43). The pairing — *anablepson* (look up, receive sight) and *he pistis sou sesoken se* (your faith has saved you) — joins physical healing to spiritual recognition. The blind man becomes the model disciple, following Jesus on the road to Jerusalem (18:43).

luke|20|45.text: 20:45 In the audience of all the people he said unto his disciples: The setting for Jesus' warning against the scribes (20:46-47). The audience is public — the people hear — but the address is to the disciples, who alone could process the indictment without indignation. Public truth, instructed in private hearing (cp. Matt 13:11).

matthew|18|33.text: 18:33 Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant: The master's rhetorical question in the parable of the unforgiving servant (18:23-35). *Edei kai se eleesai* — was it not necessary for you also to have mercy — frames forgiveness as logical duty for the forgiven. The kingdom-grammar of mercy is not optional but axiomatic.

nehemiah|7|63.text: 7:63 Of the priests: the children of Habaiah, the children of Koz, the children of Barzillai: Three priestly families whose registry was disputed. Barzillai had married into the lay Barzillai of Gilead — David's old supporter (2 Sam 17:27) — and taken that name. Genealogical purity for priestly service was strictly defended; this family had ambiguous standing.

nehemiah|7|64.text: 7:64 These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but it was not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood: The unregistered priests were excluded until divine judgment could clarify (7:65). The strict precedent expresses what Ezra and Nehemiah valued — covenant identity was traceable, not merely claimed (cp. Ezra 2:62-63; Mal 2:7-8).

nehemiah|7|67.text: 7:67 Beside their manservants and their maidservants, of whom there were seven thousand three hundred thirty and seven: The household tally adds 7,337 servants to the 42,360 freed returnees (7:66). Add the 200 singers and the totals match Ezra 2:64-65 closely. The numbers preserve the scale of the restoration — a small but real nation, not a token group.

nehemiah|11|27.text: 11:27 At Hazar-shual, and at Beer-sheba, and in the villages thereof: A list of Judahite towns repopulated after the exile. *Hazar-shual* and *Beer-sheba* mark the southern frontier of Judah's reach, evidence that the restoration was not confined to Jerusalem but spread into rebuilt town life across the territory (cp. Josh 19:3).

nehemiah|11|29.text: 11:29 At En-rimmon, and at Zareah, and at Jarmuth: Three more rebuilt towns. *En-rimmon* (the spring of Rimmon) appears in Josh 15:32; *Zareah* — Samson's hometown (Judg 13:25) — is restored; *Jarmuth* echoes its premonarchic identity (Josh 10:3). Post-exilic resettlement deliberately reclaimed historic towns.

nehemiah|11|34.text: 11:34 Hadid, Zeboim, Neballat: Benjaminite towns in the Shephelah and central highlands. *Hadid* (cp. Ezra 2:33) and *Neballat* (unknown elsewhere) reflect the geographical limits of the returned Benjaminites — a smaller foothold than pre-exile but a genuine renewed presence in the ancestral territory.

numbers|10|34.text: 10:34 The cloud of the Lord was upon them by day, when they went out of the camp: The departing march from Sinai (10:11-33) is accompanied by the *anan YHWH* — the cloud over the camp throughout the wilderness journey (cp. Exod 13:21-22; Num 9:15-23). Divine guidance was not metaphor but visible reality, the marching pillar leading every step.

numbers|13|28.text: 13:28 Nevertheless the people be strong that dwell in the land, and the cities are walled, and very great: The spies' report begins truthfully — the land's inhabitants are formidable. But the *efes* (nevertheless) opens onto fear rather than faith. The same data could have spurred trust in God's promise; the ten spies turn it into reason for retreat (cp. 13:31-33; Heb 3:19).

numbers|21|32.text: 21:32 Moses sent to spy out Jaazer, and they took the villages thereof: The eastern conquest continues. *Yazer* — northeast of Heshbon — falls without prolonged campaign, recorded in a single verse. The narrative compresses several Amorite victories to focus on the larger battle with Bashan and Og in the following chapter.

numbers|26|13.text: 26:13 Of Zerah, the family of the Zarhites: of Shaul, the family of the Shaulites: Final clans of Simeon at the second-year census (26:12-14). The tribe's total (22,200) had shrunk dramatically from the first census (59,300 in Num 1:23), reflecting the harsh consequences of the Baal-Peor incident in which Simeon featured prominently (cp. Num 25:14).

numbers|26|14.text: 26:14 These are the families of the Simeonites, twenty and two thousand and two hundred: The diminished Simeonite count — the smallest tribal total at this census. The dramatic shrinkage signals the lethal effect of plague and judgment on Simeon in particular; Jacob's deathbed prophecy of Simeon's scattering (Gen 49:7) begins to be realized.

numbers|26|16.text: 26:16 Of Ozni, the family of the Oznites: of Eri, the family of the Erites: Continuing the Gadite clans (26:15-17). The Gadites' total — 40,500 (26:18) — represents a slight reduction from the first census (45,650 in Num 1:25), more stable than Simeon but still touched by the wilderness years.

numbers|26|17.text: 26:17 Of Arod, the family of the Arodites: of Areli, the family of the Arelites: The closing two Gadite clans. The careful enumeration of seven Gadite sub-families establishes the territorial claims that will divide Gad's portion east of Jordan after Sihon's defeat (cp. Num 32; Josh 13:24-28).

numbers|26|18.text: 26:18 These are the families of the children of Gad according to those that were numbered of them, forty thousand and five hundred: Gad's total at the second census. The decrease of about 5,000 since the first census (Num 1:25) reflects ordinary attrition more than judgment — Gad came through the wilderness years with relatively stable numbers.

numbers|26|20.text: 26:20 The sons of Judah after their families were; of Shelah, the family of the Shelanites: Judah's three major clans (26:20-22) — Shelah, Pharez, Zerah. Pharez's descendants will subdivide further (26:21) because his line carries the royal-Davidic-messianic future (cp. Ruth 4:18-22; Matt 1:3).

numbers|26|21.text: 26:21 The sons of Pharez were; of Hezron, the family of the Hezronites: of Hamul, the family of the Hamulites: Pharez's two sons — Hezron and Hamul — found sub-families. Hezron will be ancestor to David through Ram (cp. Ruth 4:18-22; Matt 1:3-6). The genealogical detail at Numbers 26 prepares the way for the monarchy and the Messiah.

numbers|26|22.text: 26:22 These are the families of Judah according to those that were numbered of them, threescore and sixteen thousand and five hundred: Judah's total — 76,500 — is the largest of any tribe at the second census. The growth from the first census (74,600 in Num 1:27) anticipates Judah's preeminence under David and the messianic promise (cp. Gen 49:10).

numbers|26|24.text: 26:24 Of Jashub, the family of the Jashubites: of Shimron, the family of the Shimronites: Two of Issachar's four clans (26:23-24). Issachar's total — 64,300 (26:25) — represents an increase from the first census (54,400 in Num 1:29), one of the few tribes that grew through the wilderness years.

numbers|26|25.text: 26:25 These are the families of Issachar according to those that were numbered of them, threescore and four thousand and three hundred: Issachar's healthy total. Jacob had described Issachar as a strong donkey couching between two burdens (Gen 49:14-15); the tribe's continued growth in spite of the wilderness reflects that quiet strength.

numbers|26|27.text: 26:27 These are the families of the Zebulunites according to those that were numbered of them, threescore thousand and five hundred: Zebulun's total — 60,500 — also up from the first census (57,400). The northern tribes generally show more stable or increased numbers, perhaps reflecting less exposure to the major judgment events in the wilderness.

numbers|26|29.text: 26:29 Of the sons of Manasseh: of Machir, the family of the Machirites: Manasseh's clans descend through Machir, his only son (Gen 50:23). Machir begat Gilead, whose clan name becomes territorial — Gilead the man and Gilead the region east of the Jordan share the same name (cp. Num 32:40).

numbers|26|30.text: 26:30 These are the sons of Gilead: of Jeezer, the family of the Jeezerites: of Helek, the family of the Helekites: The Gileadite sub-clans, the inheritance of Manasseh east of Jordan. The detailed division here lays groundwork for the eastern allotment that follows the conquest of Sihon and Og.

numbers|26|31.text: 26:31 Of Asriel, the family of the Asrielites: and of Shechem, the family of the Shechemites: Three more Gileadite clans. *Shechem* — also a major Canaanite city in the central highlands — preserves a name that crosses tribal and territorial boundaries; the personal Shechem here is distinct from the city.

numbers|26|32.text: 26:32 Of Shemida, the family of the Shemidaites: and of Hepher, the family of the Hepherites: The final two clans of Gilead. Hepher will be remembered as the grandfather of Zelophehad (26:33), whose daughters' inheritance case (Num 27:1-11) sets a major legal precedent in Israelite property law.

numbers|26|34.text: 26:34 These are the families of Manasseh, and those that were numbered of them, fifty and two thousand and seven hundred: Manasseh's total — 52,700 — is striking as one of the largest gains since the first census (32,200 in Num 1:34). Jacob's blessing that Manasseh too would become a people (Gen 48:19) finds documented increase in this register.

numbers|26|36.text: 26:36 These are the sons of Shuthelah: of Eran, the family of the Eranites: Ephraim's clans through Shuthelah, Becher, and Tahan (26:35). The names will recur in 1 Chr 7:20-21; Ephraim's territorial weight in the central highlands matched the prominent role Ephraim played among the tribes (cp. Hos 4:17; 5:3).

numbers|26|37.text: 26:37 These are the families of the sons of Ephraim according to those that were numbered of them, thirty and two thousand and five hundred. These are the sons of Joseph after their families: Ephraim's total — 32,500, down from 40,500 (Num 1:33). Together with Manasseh's gain, the two tribes of Joseph form a substantial coalition that will dominate the northern kingdom after the schism.

numbers|26|39.text: 26:39 Of Shupham, the family of the Shuphamites: of Hupham, the family of the Huphamites: Two Benjaminite clans (26:38-41). Benjamin's count of 45,600 (26:41) is up from 35,400 (Num 1:37), a major increase reflecting recovery from the catastrophic civil war that nearly extinguished the tribe (cp. Judg 20:46-48).

numbers|26|40.text: 26:40 The sons of Bela were Ard and Naaman: of Ard, the family of the Ardites: and of Naaman, the family of the Naamites: Sub-clans descending from Bela, Benjamin's firstborn. The careful sub-division testifies to Benjamin's recovery from near-extinction at Gibeah and prepares for the territory the tribe will hold north of Judah, including Jerusalem (cp. Josh 18:11-28).

numbers|26|41.text: 26:41 These are the sons of Benjamin after their families: and they that were numbered of them were forty and five thousand and six hundred: Benjamin's total — 45,600 — caps the recovery from civil-war-era depletion. The tribe will produce Saul, Jeremiah, Mordecai, and Paul, its small size offset by outsized influence (cp. Phil 3:5; Rom 11:1).

numbers|26|43.text: 26:43 All the families of the Shuhamites, according to those that were numbered of them, were threescore and four thousand and four hundred: Dan's lone son Shuham (or Hushim; cp. Gen 46:23) founded the only Danite clan, yet the tribe's total — 64,400 — is the second-largest after Judah. Concentrated lineage produced disproportionate numbers, perhaps reflecting strong inter-marriage within the tribe.

numbers|26|45.text: 26:45 Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the family of the Heberites: of Malchiel, the family of the Malchielites: Two grandsons of Asher (Beriah's sons) found sub-clans. Beriah's name — *bera'ah* (in calamity) — preserves a family origin story of crisis, but the line flourished in the wilderness years.

numbers|26|46.text: 26:46 The name of the daughter of Asher was Sarah: An unusual notice of a daughter in an otherwise male-only register. *Serakh* (variant of Sarah) reappears in 1 Chr 7:30 with her brothers, and Jewish tradition gave her remarkable longevity. The verse preserves the memory that women were not absent from tribal identity.

numbers|26|47.text: 26:47 These are the families of the sons of Asher according to those that were numbered of them; who were fifty and three thousand and four hundred: Asher's total — 53,400, up from 41,500 (Num 1:41) — represents one of the largest tribal gains since the wilderness began. Jacob's blessing of *rich food* for Asher (Gen 49:20) seems to have nourished a flourishing line.

numbers|26|49.text: 26:49 Of Jezer, the family of the Jezerites: of Shillem, the family of the Shillemites: Two of Naphtali's four clans (26:48-49). Naphtali's count (45,400; 26:50) is slightly down from 53,400 (Num 1:43), one of the more typical tribal shrinkages over the wilderness years.

numbers|26|50.text: 26:50 These are the families of Naphtali according to their families: and they that were numbered of them were forty and five thousand and four hundred: Naphtali's total. The cumulative census (601,730; cp. 26:51) shows the total fighting-age men only marginally smaller than the first count — Israel preserved its broad numbers through judgment, ready for conquest.

numbers|27|23.text: 27:23 He laid his hands upon him, and gave him a charge: Moses' commissioning of Joshua follows the Lord's instruction (27:18-21). The hand-laying is the same gesture later used in priestly consecration (Lev 8:14, 18) and in ordination of elders (1 Tim 4:14; 5:22) — succession in office made visible by physical transfer of authority.

numbers|33|33.text: 33:33 They went from Hor-hagidgad, and pitched in Jotbathah: Two stations in the southern wilderness journey. *Yotvatah* — variously identified, possibly on the western side of the Wadi Arabah — was a place of streams (cp. Deut 10:7), a hint of provision in otherwise harsh terrain.

numbers|33|34.text: 33:34 They removed from Jotbathah, and encamped at Ebronah: The Ebronah encampment, location unknown today, continues the southern circuit toward Ezion-geber (33:35). The careful itinerary list — forty-two stations — preserves the geography of the wilderness years as the basis of Israel's historical memory.

numbers|33|41.text: 33:41 They departed from mount Hor, and pitched in Zalmonah: After Aaron's death (33:38-39), the people leave Mount Hor and resume the southeastern circuit toward Moab. *Tsalmonah* — also unidentified — opens the final segment of the wilderness journey, the approach to the plains of Moab and Jericho.

numbers|33|49.text: 33:49 They pitched by Jordan, from Beth-jesimoth even unto Abel-shittim in the plains of Moab: The final encampment of the wilderness years. *Abel-shittim* — the meadow of acacias — is the staging area for the conquest (cp. Num 25:1; Josh 2:1; 3:1). The journey ends on the eastern bank of the Jordan, the Promised Land in view.

numbers|34|29.text: 34:29 These are they whom the Lord commanded to divide the inheritance unto the children of Israel in the land of Canaan: The closing summary of the tribal princes (34:17-28) appointed to oversee land distribution. Eleazar the priest and Joshua the leader head the commission (34:17), but each tribe sends its own prince — fairness and tribal voice built into the allotment process.

psalms|59|17.text: 59:17 Unto thee, O my strength, will I sing: for God is my defence, and the God of my mercy: The psalm's closing doxology. The triple title — *uzzi* (my strength), *misgabbi* (my high tower), and *Elohei hasdi* (the God of my steadfast love) — gathers David's experience of rescue (from Saul; cp. 1 Sam 19:11) into song. Praise rises out of preserved life.

psalms|80|19.text: 80:19 Turn us again, O Lord God of hosts, cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved: The threefold refrain (cp. 80:3, 7) closes the psalm with the same petition that has shaped it. *Hashivenu* (turn us, restore us) names the work only God can do — both the people's return and the Lord's face shining are gifts received, not achievements (cp. Num 6:25; Lam 5:21).

psalms|81|16.text: 81:16 He should have fed them also with the finest of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee: The psalm's poignant closing — the abundance Israel would have known had they listened (81:13). The conditional *had they* leaves the abundance unrealized; the verse mourns what disobedience forfeits even from a God who longs to give (cp. Deut 32:13-14; Isa 1:19-20).

psalms|84|12.text: 84:12 O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man that trusteth in thee: The psalm's third beatitude (cp. 84:4, 5). *Ashre adam botah-bakh* (blessed is the one who trusts in you) names the deepest theme of the psalm — the joy of pilgrimage to the courts of the Lord rests on confidence in him. The final word is trust, not the temple itself.

psalms|109|31.text: 109:31 He shall stand at the right hand of the poor, to save him from those that condemn his soul: The closing affirmation of one of the imprecatory psalms. *Yikhom liyemin* (he shall stand at the right hand) reverses the courtroom imagery of 109:6 (where Satan stood at the wicked man's right hand to accuse). God himself becomes the helper at the poor's right hand (cp. Ps 16:8; 73:23; Rom 8:34).

psalms|118|27.text: 118:27 God is the Lord, which hath shewed us light: bind the sacrifice with cords, even unto the horns of the altar: Light from God (cp. Num 6:25; Ps 27:1) prompts the festal procession to the altar. *Isru-khag baavotim* (bind the festival with cords) names a ritual still observed in Jewish festivals; the verb gathers Israel into the very moment of joyful sacrifice.

psalms|118|28.text: 118:28 Thou art my God, and I will praise thee: thou art my God, I will exalt thee: The doubled affirmation — *Eli atta* (you are my God) — frames the climactic individual response within the great hallel (Pss 113-118). The phrase compresses the entire covenant — possession and confession running both directions (cp. Hos 2:23).

psalms|118|29.text: 118:29 O give thanks unto the Lord; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever: The psalm closes by echoing its opening (118:1) — the same liturgical formula that bookends much of Israel's praise (cp. Pss 106:1; 107:1; 1 Chr 16:34). *Hesed* (steadfast love) endures forever; the doxology is the only fitting close.

psalms|121|8.text: 121:8 The Lord shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore: The pilgrim psalm closes with the complete temporal sweep — every movement (going out, coming in) and every duration (from now into eternity). *Tsetkha uvo'ekha* names the totality of life's traffic. God's preserving care covers all of it, without lapse.

song-of-solomon|3|4.text: 3:4 I held him, and would not let him go: The beloved's grasp at finding the loved one. *Akhaztiv velo arpennu* (I held him and would not let go) becomes a vivid figure throughout Christian devotion for the soul's hold on Christ (cp. Jacob's wrestling, Gen 32:26; Mary's clinging in John 20:17). Spiritual longing seeks tangible communion.

song-of-solomon|3|5.text: 3:5 I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field: The recurring refrain (cp. 2:7; 8:4). The oath formula — by gazelles and hinds — has more poetry than legal force, but the substance is plain: love is not to be hurried. The repeated charge insists on patience until the right moment.

song-of-solomon|4|7.text: 4:7 Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee: The lover's summary praise. *Kullakh yafah ra'yati* (you are all beautiful, my love) becomes one of the verses most often applied to the church by patristic and medieval Christian readers (cp. Eph 5:27 — without spot or wrinkle). The bride is loved as wholly cherished.

song-of-solomon|4|15.text: 4:15 A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon: The lover names the beloved's gift to him in language Jesus will adopt for himself (John 4:14; 7:38). *Mayim hayyim* (living waters) is a Hebrew term for spring-fed flowing water, not stagnant — fresh and constantly renewed.

song-of-solomon|7|3.text: 7:3 Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins: The wasf — a descriptive love-poem cataloguing the beloved's beauties — uses pastoral imagery throughout the chapter. The doubled gazelles (cp. 4:5) figure tenderness and balanced beauty rather than mere physical detail; Hebrew love-poetry was earthy without being crude.

song-of-solomon|7|10.text: 7:10 I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me: The closing covenantal formula of the Song — mutual belonging woven with desire. *Ani ledodi vealay teshukato* echoes 2:16 and 6:3, but here adds *teshuqah* (desire) — the same word used of Eve's desire in Gen 3:16, here restored to right relation between lovers.

song-of-solomon|8|7.text: 8:7 Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: One of the Song's most quoted lines. *Mayim rabbim* (many waters) is a stock biblical image for chaos and threat (cp. Ps 29:3; 93:4); the verse declares love stronger than the cosmic dangers themselves. Love's commerce cannot be reduced to purchase; it is given or it is nothing.
